speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ILLICIT TRAFFICKING-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), announced the National Drug Strategy which sets a uniquely Canadian course in dealing with the problems posed by drug abuse and illicit trafficking. It recognizes the excellent work done by the RCMP, by Customs and Excise and by other law enforcement agencies in preventing the importation and trafficking of drugs.
In general, the programs of the strategy are directed at solving domestic problems in Canada. However, illicit trafficking is an international industry and it is clear that
Canada cannot solve our drug abuse and trafficking problems in isolation.
Many of the drugs consumed in Canada such as cocaine and heroin are brought into our country illegally by well organized trafficking networks based overseas. In 1985, the RCMP and Customs seized 62 kilograms of heroin, 109 kilograms of cocaine and 19,000 kilograms of hashish. These are the last statistics available for 1985 and they probably understate the dimensions of the problem today.
Furthermore, Canadian territory often serves as a transit point for narcotics being sent by these trafficking networks to other countries. In addition to that, illicit psychoactive substances are produced in Canada to feed the terrible addictions of citizens of other countries. Clearly we must act to stem this traffic, not only because Canadians are its victims but also because we have a role to play as responsible citizens of the world.

Drug abuse is not a new phenomenon, but its extent is indeed. As early as in 1909 Canada participated actively in drafting an international convention on the control of opium trafficking. And today still we continue to play a major role within such United Nations bodies as the Commission on Narcotic Drugs. Yesterday, as a matter of fact, Canada was re-elected to this important commission which in past years had concentrated its efforts specially on the problem of supply reduction.
Along with other countries Canada played a part in the introduction of a new element in the approach taken by the Commission, namely the reduction of demand. We are also trying to take into account certain other elements such as the new complexity of international networks of traffickers.

Their tentacles now stretching around the world, these networks have refined their procedures for moving their product. Some utilize couriers who, travelling by air, carry the drugs strapped to their bodies. Other shipments are disguised as cargoes of innocuous commodities. The profits earned by this illicit enterprise are protected by a variety of methods, the use of shell companies and other means. The money earned from drug trafficking is sent to offshore havens.
These problems can only be faced effectively through international co-operation so the UN Commission is preparing a new international convention on illicit trafficking. The origin

May 28, 1987
Statements by Ministers
of this convention is a resolution of the UN General Assembly co-sponsored by Canada and adopted in December, 1984. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), served as a member of the Canadian delegation to the UN and announced Canada's co-sponsorship of that important international initiative. This new convention can become a powerful tool for law enforcement agencies around the world to use against traffickers. Canada places a high priority on successful completion of the new convention.
The Government is working internationally on three other fronts. The UN Fund for Drug Abuse Control sponsors projects which assist producer countries to develop and finance programs that will help farmers move away from drug production, help improve local standards of living, and help train local police to deal with the extremely well-organized drug traffickers. Canada has made substantial contributions to this body's general fund as well as giving two grants of $1 million apiece to UNFDAC projects in Thailand and Pakistan to develop alternative crops for farmers. That is a new policy direction for C1DA established in 1986. As well, we will continue to consider on a case-by-case basis requests from narcotics-producing countries for development assistance.
Second, our contribution to UNFDAC will be raised to $500,000 this year and $1 million by 1991 to demonstrate our commitment to international co-operation.
Third, we are expanding the consular awareness program of the Department of External Affairs to make Canadian travellers more aware of the dangers of drug purchase, drug possession, drug trafficking, and drug use abroad. Sir, more Canadians are in prison overseas for drug offences than for any other crime.
A UN sponsored international conference on drug abuse and illicit trafficking will take place in Vienna from June 17 to June 26. Our delegates to this conference will be led by my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). In order to reflect truly the international approach of this Government to the issue of drug abuse the delegation will also include representatives from the provinces and the voluntary sector.

Canada played a significant role in drafting the 1971 convention on psychotropic substances. When in Vienna the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) will be tabling the accession instruments which will make it possible to enforce this convention here in Canada.
The Government acknowledges that wide-ranging efforts will be made in Canada to fight drug abuse and traffic. We also believe that if we choose to ignore the international aspects we will be doing so at our own risk. The part of our national drug strategy which relates to the international aspects attests to our intention to co-operate with other countries to reduce drug production, traffic and abuse both in Canada and abroad.

subsubtopic: ILLICIT TRAFFICKING-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think today's announcement is another example of the Government's position on the drug question, much ado about nothing. I refer specifically to the Minister's announcement that we will be increasing the amount of money we give to the UN Fund for Drug Abuse Control. In the past it was the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) who was responsible for funding our contribution to UNFDAC, which is indeed doing very important work as outlined by the Minister. At the beginning of this year that Department refused to continue paying that funding because they said it was a problem for the Department of External Affairs. The Department of External Affairs said it would not pay for our contribution, which at that point was just under $400,000, because it was a health and welfare problem. We played financial ping-pong on this issue for several months until finally, this week, we get word from the Government that, yes, its contribution to UNFDAC will continue and will indeed be increased. It is now, presumably, covered by the Department of External Affairs.
We were trying to get information as late as last week about whether the Government had taken up its responsibility to contribute to UNFDAC, but we could not get an answer from the Minister. We could not get an answer from External Affairs. We could not get an answer from Health and Welfare. As is typical of this Government, they were passing the buck. Health and Welfare said it was an international problem which should be funded through External Affairs. We now finally see that the Government is going to move in this area and for that we are grateful, but there is one area of the UN convention where the Government has unfortunately chosen not to act.
We heard the Minister talk today about the difficulty in stemming the increase in the flow of illicit drugs into Canada. Indeed, over the course of the last several months the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare heard from the RCMP and those involved in the interdiction of international trafficking, that indeed stemming the inflow of drugs into any country is practically impossible. We have to attack it from the demand as well as the supply end. However, there is one area where the Government could have acted and it would have followed up on the UN convention which is being developed. It could even have followed the example of the U.S., which it is prone to do, concerning what happens to drug profits. What happens to the money laundered through legitimate sources, including some Canadian banks, whether it be here in Canada or offshore?
We have heard questions in the House over the last number of months about why the Canadian Government did not introduce legislation to permit the seizure of assets gained through illegal methods. In order to stop the drug trade you have to make it less profitable. It is fine for the Minister to stand in the House and talk about illegal drugs coming into the country. We know that. We know that if we stem the tide of drugs coming in to Nova Scotia from offshore it may indeed
May 28, 1987

spring up in another area of the country. However, if the Government had the political courage to introduce legislation to force Canadian banks to give up money received through illegal drug trafficking, if it had the political courage to say to Canadian banks that they could not receive laundered money, then we would start getting to the root of the problem.
Unfortunately, the Government has not had the courage to do that. In fact, notwithstanding the UN convention which is being developed, Canada again has blinkers on. Canada is going to be the last to get on board, just as it was the last to get on board this year with the UNFDAC contribution.

Nevertheless, I am glad to see that the Government is going to do something about the matter of psychotropic drugs. I think Canada was a leader in 1971, when the UN International Convention was drafted, but when it was signed in 1976, Canada was not a signatory. I think that we, that the previous Liberal Government should have signed the Convention to try and control the question of psychotropic drugs.
However, I want to warn the Minister that psychotropic drugs are not just the drugs that come to Canada.
We should log the Government's action in the area of psychotropic drugs. I wish that the previous Liberal Government had signed the convention which we were instrumental in beginning to develop in 1971, but it did not, and the Government is rectifying that.
I would like the Minister to be aware that the question of psychotropic substances is not only dealt with in the illegal drugs which are coming into the country, but also in drugs that are being made in Canada. I refer to recent press reports which show that in Montreal legal drugs are being garnered through the Canadian health system and sold as quaaludes, illegal drugs, in the United States. It is a very serious problem.
We also need to have answers on the question of designer drugs. I hope that when the Government introduces specific legislation following the UN Convention on Psychotropic Substances it will include the area of designer drugs.

The most important thing is, Mr. Speaker, that if the Government-if the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark)-is truly prepared to act, to fight against drugs, it will have to introduce, through the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), certain amendments that will enable the federal Government to seize funds now in Canadian banks, whether here in Canada or abroad, and I am referring to profits made from drug trafficking.
Statements by Ministers

If we are unprepared to seize assets garnered by illegal drug trade which are currently on deposit in Canadian banks, then all the money we are giving to UNFDAC, all of the work we are doing here, and the measures which have been announced by the Minister will be for naught. As long as there is a profit to be made from the drug trade and as long as there are Canadians who continue to use legal and illegal drugs, there will continue to be a problem. We must attack it from the demand side. In terms of the supply side we must definitely introduce legislation to permit us to seize assets from Canadian banks. Without that legislation all this talk is only puffery.

subsubtopic: ILLICIT TRAFFICKING-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before specifically addressing the announcement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) I would like to weigh the attack on drug abuse in terms of attacks on the supply versus the demand side. In examining the new drug strategy within the context of the demand side we must call attention to the fact that although a great deal of emphasis continues to be placed upon illicit drugs, street drugs, and over-the-counter prescription drugs, the same factors operate in impelling the use of the most dangerous and widely used drug, namely alcohol.
In addressing the issue of demand it is clear that essentially the same factors operate in the overuse of alcohol as in the overuse of over-the-counter drugs, marijuana, and other street drugs which are frequently abused. Having said that, it is certainly clear that immense tragedy is caused through the use of drugs which are exchanged internationally, whether drugs derived from opium, such as cocaine, or some of the new synthetic drugs which are subject to abuse.
The program announced by the Government is impressive on first sight. We are told that $210 million will be spent over the next five years. However, we must put that and the entire program in perspective. In the first year only $20 million is to be spent. When you really think about it, $210 million is not an awful lot of money considering the immensity of the problem that we are attempting to attack.
Furthermore, we have a concern about the distribution of that money and its focus with respect to the essentials of the problem. I rose in this House the other day to express concern about the fact that this program was announced without reference to the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare which is engaged in an examination of the issue of alcohol and drug abuse. I was pleased to hear from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) that the recommendations of that committee will be taken into account as the National Drug Strategy develops its specifics. I hope that that promise will be met. I hope we will have an opportunity to scrutinize this program with a fine tooth comb to ensure its effectiveness.
In terms of the record of the past Liberal Government and what has happened heretofore, we welcome the program announced this morning by the Secretary of State for External

May 28, 1987
Tabling of Documents
Affairs. In many respects it is long past due. The accession to the international Convention on Psychotropic Substances which was approved in 1971 pleases us immensely. Canada's contribution heretofore to the UN Fund for Drug Abuse Control amounted to $300,000. This will be raised to $500,000, and we of course welcome that. We welcome the somewhat more tenuous promise that this will be raised to $ 1 million by 1991. However, we must put this in perspective as well. Italy, for example, is contributing something in the order of $300 million for the same purpose.
We know that these funds are designed to help bring about economic changes which will take farmers in the Third World away from drug production and divert them to the cultivation of more useful crops. This entails economic changes which will enable those Third World countries to adapt to new circumstances. When we analyse that situation we see that the Third World is once again being exploited to its disadvantage. Considerably more effort must be exerted to make it possible for Third World countries and ordinary farmers there to prosper without being involved in the cultivation of drugs which do harm in those countries as well as in Canada.
I am under the impression that this program will not divert funds from CIDA which are allocated for essentially the same purpose. I would be very disturbed if funds were diverted from CIDA to accomplish the same purpose.
Expanding consular awareness of the dangers of being involved in drug usage in foreign countries when travelling is laudable, although I am not so sure of how significant it is. One would have to measure that against the failure to address the issue of AIDS with alacrity. I think that is a far more serious problem. Although I recognize that while travellers will not become addicts through a 10 day or two-week exploration of these agents in foreign countries, it is true that they may find themselves in serious difficulty.
We must address the issue of laundered money and the attempt to control it. We understand that there will be legislation introduced in the House tomorrow to address the problem of money being diverted through financial institutions into legitimate concerns which hides the existence of moneys earned through the illicit drug trade. However, I cannot possibly understand how a Government which wants to be taken seriously on the issue of laundering money earned through the illicit drug trade would fail to address the need for the reporting of funds deposited or internationally exchanged. This is done very effectively in the United States and ensures that they will have the means of detecting the fact that this money is gained from the illicit drug trade and the use of that money for other purposes, which subsequently makes it impossible to track down. If the Government is serious, then it will immediately introduce legislation comparable to that in the United States which has been so potent in dealing with the problem of laundered money derived from the sale of illicit drugs.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of tabling the First Report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade.
In this report, the committee has tried to set forth the objectives and directions of our official development assistance program for the next several years. We suggest a change of focus to human development and human resource development. We urge a greater emphasis on human rights. We urge, in the strongest possible terms, a major decentralization to the field. In fact, "out of Ottawa to the field" is a thought that runs throughout the whole report.
We make new proposals about tied aid. We support an increased role for the non-governmental organizations, institutions and business. We think that, on the whole, we have responded to the concerns expressed to us by Canadians and people in other countries.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext:
That this House oppose any imposition of a federal tax on food and urge the Government to reject any such tax as part of its tax reform package.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that this debate is necessary today. It would not have been necessary had the Government been more clear about its intentions when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) made his statement on tax reform on May 6.
As it is, the Government is continuing to play games with the Canadian consumers and families with average incomes across the country about whether it will carry through with its intention to put a 6 per cent or 8 per cent sales tax on the family grocery bill for every Canadian family. That is the issue and the reason that I and my Party are asking members of all Parties to join with the New Democrats in making it very clear that the House should oppose any imposition of a federal tax on food and urge the Government to reject any such tax as part of its tax reform package.
The reason for scheduling the debate now is simple. When the Minister of Finance outlined his plans and gave the House a preview of what he would be exposing on June 18, I warned him that he would be facing a tax revolt from New Democrats and Canadians from coast to coast if the Government carried out its intention to impose a business transfer tax that included food. We want there to be no mistake about this issue and that is why today's debate is so important.
Let me outline exactly what is at stake. For the past two years the Minister of Finance and the Government have been inching toward a comprehensive package of tax reform. The Finance Minister indicates that he wants to bring personal and corporate tax rates down in Canada to around the levels that are now being levied in the United States after its recent tax reform.
There are two ways in which he wants to gain the revenues to accomplish that. As we understand it, he intends to broaden the tax base by eliminating tax loopholes and unproductive tax deductions and exemptions. The Americans succeeded in lowering their tax rates in that way, broadening the base at the same time.
The Canadian tax system has a heavier burden to bear than in the United States, mainly because we have a more comprehensive and adequate structure of social services, particularly medicare. Canadians would not want it any different.
However, as the Finance Minister comes to grips with this particular problem it appears that he is now intending to take a major amount of new revenues from the sale tax system.

May 28, 1987
Supply
He has indicated for some time that he wishes to reform Canada's antiquated sales tax system, the federal manufacturers' sales tax. The NDP agrees that that tax is long overdue for reform. In its present form, it tends to give a tax break to importers bringing goods into Canadian markets and, at the same time, tends to discriminate against Canadian exporters who lose an edge when competing against other countries which more effectively rebate sales taxes from their exports.
The motivation which has led the Minister to embrace the concept of sales tax reform is the prospect of major increases in federal revenues which would then allow him to cut the personal and corporate tax rates. In this way he hopes to emerge as the hero who saved the fortunes of the Conservative Party and enabled it to return as a minority Government rather than simply becoming a one-term Government and a brief blip in the political history of this country, despite their enormous victory in 1984.
The Minister of Finance, and I have said this before, has been playing a shell game with Canadian taxpayers. He is trying to come up a hero by saying: "Look at what I have done", in terms of reducing the personal tax rates when he makes his announcements on the evening of June 18. At the same time he is not prepared to have Canadians look at what they will be paying in additional taxes or what the inflationary impact will be of the broadening and increasing of the sales tax system as is apparently being contemplated by the Government.
The present manufacturers' sales tax covers only about 32 per cent of Canada's economy, that is, that two-thirds of the goods and services which are sold every year, or the value-added in the economy, are exempt from this tax. This means that the tax discriminates against manufactured goods in favour of services and that it is unduly high because there are so many areas not covered. In other words, the present revenue of about $16 billion from the sales tax could be achieved with a rate of only 6 per cent or so, if all goods and services were taxed rather than only some.
A 1 per cent rate in the proposed business transfer tax would give the Government a revenue of about $2.6 billion. What is happening is that I think the Minister of Finance has allowed himself to be seduced. He has been seduced not in the sense that might embarrass him politically, as has happened recently in the United States, but he has been seduced in the sense that it could be very adverse politically. He has been seduced by the technocrats in the Department of Finance who themselves are convinced that, for technical reasons, what Canada should have is a business transfer tax, which applies as much to people's weekly grocery bill at Safeway, Loblaws, the IGA or at their independent food store, as to the purchase of a car or a lawyer's service. They want to apply it to such things as people's payments for day care. I am not sure if they want to
apply it to dentists' bills. We have not seen what the exemptions might be. However, clearly, the fewer the exemptions the happier the advisers to the Minister are going to be.
The Government has carefully worded a statement on this particular subject which was designed to be uninformative. I accuse the Minister of Finance of being the Gypsy Rose Lee of tax reform. I am reminded of those fan dancers who used to flourish back in the 1920s and 1930s. Every time they were about to expose all by throwing a fan into the air, they would tactfully put another fan just in front of the naughty bits. That is what the Minister of Finance has been doing with respect to his proposals for the sales tax.
The Minister of Finance is talking about the creation of a "broad-based, multi-stage sales tax". Who on earth could be opposed to that? Who in fact could understand exactly what that means. When we asked more detailed questions, we were put off. We were told: "No, the Government is not backing off from its intentions to reform the sales tax. It is only laying out three optional ways by which the sales tax can be collected". Lo and behold, when we look at it more carefully, the plans of the tax experts in the Department of Finance to tax food, are still there front and centre. It is still to be repudiated by the Government.
As the Minister of Finance put it, his first option remains the business transfer tax. He calls it a "federal tax only without invoices". He calls it a "goods and services tax". He says: "It is relatively simple both to administer and to comply with but only if it is applied uniformly on all goods and services". There is no mistaking what that means. It means that sales tax would be applied on food as well as on every other article of service which businesses and consumers purchase.
This also means that this tax is misnamed if it is being called a "business transfer tax". It is a consumer tax. It is a tax which will be paid by consumers. It is not a business tax. It is not a substitute for adequate increases in corporation or profit taxes. People will save a few dollars on their personal income tax, but will end up paying hundreds of dollars more in sales tax and will be worse off rather than better.
I grant that other options are being considered. A federal-provincial sales tax is one suggestion. The Government has also been talking about a value-added tax along the European model which would permit more discrimination between different types of goods being taxed. However, there are a lot of hurdles in the way of these two particular proposals. Not all the provinces have jumped for joy at the prospect of a joint tax. One of the reasons for that, of course, is that they feel it is important that they be able to carry out some measure of provincial fiscal policy by means of the exemptions in the areas in which they tax in the sales tax field.
In Quebec I believe it is still the case that soft goods, furniture, for example, are not taxed by a sales tax system because of the fact that those goods are important to Quebecers and it is a way in which the Quebec Government benefits
May 28, 1987

an important local industry and its consumers in the process. That would probably not be permitted under a joint federal-provincial sales tax.
1 think it could be very embarrassing as well if the federal-provincial sales tax were to range between a rate of, say, 6 per cent or 7 per cent in Alberta, if Alberta continued not to have any provincial sales tax, and as much as 14 per cent or 15 per cent in Newfoundland. I think a combined invisible tax like that could easily lead to a great deal of illegal but still threatening tax evasion.
The other prospect is the value-added tax. That, of course, has been resisted very strongly by small businesses which fear the paper work and which also fear the prospect of being made into a million strong army of tax collectors for the Minister of Finance and the Conservative Government. In other words, from what we can see, the Government is still intent on this food tax despite the reaction from coast to coast that this is not a tax which Canadians are prepared to support.
What is the impact of the Government's proposal? We estimated, based on a very conservative average of $5,000 in expenditures on food for an average family in a year, that the proposed tax would cost about $300 per family. This was assuming a 6 per cent tax rate. In the last three weeks I have had a chance to look at some of the work of the experts in the accounting industry and elsewhere. They are now talking about an 8 per cent tax rate for the business transfer tax. Right away the levy is up to about $400 in additional tax which will be paid on food by the average family.
The experts indicate more and more that the Government is going to be looking not for a tax-neutral prospect but for increased revenues from the sales tax, which revenues currently total about $16 billion. That might mean that the rate could easily come in as high as 9 per cent or 10 per cent rather than 8 per cent. From the food industry, that is, farmers, producers, retailers and ultimately consumers, it is estimated that the tax proposed by the Government, or this particular option available to the Government, would result in a $4 billion tax levy on one of the absolute essentials of life for Canadians.
It is hard to avoid paying for rent or housing costs. Nevertheless, one could at least argue that many Canadians do have some options if they find they have difficulty meeting housing costs. If they happen to have a home of their own, they could take in a lodger. They may not like it. It is not the Canadian way these days, but that is one way. They could also move into a smaller apartment. That is not desirable, but it is a possibility.

We cannot ask a family to do that. We cannot say to a family: "Your kids are going to have to live on macaroni and cheese for now and for the next year because of a sales tax which is being imposed by the Minister of Finance".

The Hon. Members suggests that I am dreaming. If I am, then I ask him why the Minister of Finance has, in response to many questions here in the House of Commons, not indicated absolutely clearly that this is no longer an option being considered by the Government. If the Government wanted to be free from charges that it was intending or considering this particular tax, then the way out was very easy and clear. Members of the Government could simply say to me: "Mike, stop getting worried. Tell your Party to stop getting worried. We are not going to do it". I hope that perhaps the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin), who I believe will speak in this debate, or perhaps the Minister of Finance, will get up in the House today to reassure us that that will be the case. If that were the result of this particular debate, then I would feel that the time of the House had been well spent on this Opposition Day motion in opposing the food tax and getting the Government to make it clear that it is no longer considering this particular measure.
The Government has suggested that the way around the problem created by taxing food is to provide a sales tax credit in order to take the burden off those families which would be most affected. We will of course have to wait until June 18 to see what the Government has in mind. But the performance up until now leaves my Party, myself and many Canadians very uneasy.
The Government says: "Look what we did. We innovated. We brought in a refundable sales tax credit of $50 per adult and $25 per child. That is directed at families earning under $15,000 per year. Are we not wonderful?" That measure does not compensate poor families for the regressive impact of the sales tax that is currently being applied. It does not compensate them for more than a portion of the increases in sales tax that have been levied by the Progressive Conservatives since coming to power just under three years ago.

May 28, 1987

In addition, the refundable sales tax credit does nothing to compensate the average Canadian family for the fact that the Conservatives have increased their tax burden by something in the order of $1,500 per year since they came to power in 1984. When the Conservatives came to power they said: "There is waste and inefficiency in Government. We will root it out". What they did instead was to bring in enormous tax increases which have been levied almost entirely on personal taxpayers and on people paying sales tax, not on corporations. In fact, we estimate that between 1984 and 1990 the increase in sales taxes on the average Canadian family alone will amount to some $20 billion on a cumulative basis.
What is significant is that the sales tax credit that is applied now does not apply to people earning over $20,000 per year. It does not apply to a family whose principal earner works at GM in Oshawa or Chrysler. It does not apply to a farmer struggling to get by and still having some income from a farm in western Canada. It does not apply to a clerk or a secretary raising a couple of kids and living in Vancouver where there are very heavy housing prices. It does not apply to a fisherman and his family on the coast of Nova Scotia or Newfoundland if their income is over $20,000 per year. It only applies to people earning less than $15,000 per year.
The poverty line in a major Canadian city is about $20,000 for a family of four. So many families in poverty are not benefiting at all from the sales tax credit. But government spokespeople have inadvertently, perhaps, let it out on many occasions that they only see this tax credit, which might amount to $300 per year, going to people earning less than $15,000 per year. Therefore all those families having trouble meeting mortgage payments of $600 a month, and all those families having trouble meeting rent for a home of $700 per month, as well as meeting the costs of transportation, food and maybe getting skates for the kids so that they can go to figure skating or play hockey, will be meeting a burden of $400 per year or more in increased sales tax with no compensation through the tax credit at all.

I have been waiting for assurance but we have seen nothing. What I have seen from the Conservatives is that they have raised the burden of sales tax and the tax burden on the average Canadian family by $1,500 per year. They have already begun to extend the sales tax to food. They have taxed candy. They have taxed potato chips. They have levied a tax on kids. They have taxed snacks. They have taxed soft drinks at a time when we are trying to encourage people to get away from drinking by taking alternatives. They have raised the excise taxes on gasoline, alcohol and tobacco.
My time is very close to being up. I would point out that the Government is wrong when its experts say that it is more progressive to give this tax credit than it is to exempt food from tax. Their own figures, which were given to me by the Department of Finance, indicate that a family earning $15,000 per year spends 20 per cent of its income on food. I think that
it is probably more. A family living on $60,000 per year spends less than 9 per cent of its income on food. Therefore a tax on food will hit the low income family much harder than it will hit the family earning much more money.
I point out that in Japan there is a taxpayers' revolt despite the fact that the proposed valued-added tax in Japan will not hit food, I point out that the value-added, or business transfer, tax may begin small but that the Government will be tempted to raise it the way it has been raised in Britain, France and other countries where it is now up to levels of 15 per cent or 16 per cent. If 8 per cent on food is intolerable, 15 per cent would be absolutely unconscionable. The Government has done little to maintain or gain public confidence, which is why New Democrats-

This is why the New Democratic Party-my Party-agrees with Canadian men and women who openly tell the Government: Time has come for you to assure us that no tax will be levied against food, that the business transfer tax will never apply to food, that each week the average Canadian family will not be forced to pay this tax which would cost $400 a year.

I have a brief question for the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker. 1 listened carefully to what he had to say. I was searching for his proposal for sales tax reform. It is easy to criticize whatever models are put in front of one with respect to sales tax reform, especially to take one of the models and speak against it for an extended period of time. But what is the Hon. Member's proposal for sales tax reform?
With respect to the food tax I want to ask the Hon. Member how adamant he is about what he said. If he does not believe in taxing food, then I would like to pin him down very categorically on that. Does he believe that we should continue our two-price approach to wheat? That is my first question.
My second question is the following. What if it were proven to him-and I am not too sure it could be proven-that it was progressive, that is, a heavier tax proportionately on the wealthy, if certain foods were taxed? Would the Hon. Member then favour a food tax in that situation?
He has given us his figures which indicate that any type of food tax would be regressive. What if there were figures and certain food products were taxed in such a way that it was progressive, that is, if we taxed the wealthy much more than the poor, then what would the Hon. Member have to say? This does not mean that the Government is contemplating a food tax. But I would like to know where the Hon. Member stands.
Would he be in favour of such a tax if it were progressive as opposed to regressive? What is his stand on the two-price wheat policy, which is tied to food? What is his proposal for tax reform?
May 28, 1987

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am impressed by the fact that the Minister should have jumped on the first opportunity to ask questions to the New Democratic Party. Yet I am deeply disappointed that at the same time the Minister did not make a statement on the Government intentions.
Since the Minister will have to leave the House during the debate, I would begin by asking him whether or not the Government intends to tax the increases. The Minister's question is as follows: Would we be supportive if it could be proven that this tax is progressive?
Well, Mr. Speaker, my answer is simply that, according to the figures given the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs by the Department of Finance officials whom I have just quoted, the 1982 report on family expenditures reveals that a family with an annual income of $60,000 spends about $5,000 a year on food. This is probably a conservative estimate, but the figures were provided by his Department. It accounts for about 9 per cent of the income of a family earning $60,000 a year. In the case of a family with an annual income ranging from $15,000 to $20,000, the corresponding figure is $3,000, or $60 a week. This represents 20 per cent of the annual earnings of a family with an income of $15,000.
In other words, a family averaging $15,000 a year spends proportionately twice as much on food as does a family with an annual income of $60,000.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in light of the remarks of the Department of Finance officials, it goes to show to what extent a tax on food can be regressive: it hits a family earning $15,000 twice as hard as another one with an income of $60,000, and this despite the fact that it is much easier for the latter to bear taxes for federal Government services.
I would suggest that if the Government wants to levy progressive taxes against high income families, then let us get them through an income tax system because, as I see it, the Minister's proposal is unlikely to produce a progressive sales tax system.
The two-price system for wheat, Mr. Speaker, does of course influence somewhat the price of bread and other wheat-derived products in Canada. That I admit. However, Mr. Speaker, it also represents a direct benefit for a major sector of our economy, namely, the farmers across this country.
That is why we support the system. The Minister asks whether the New Democratic Party is opposed to any taxes being levied either directly or indirectly on food. That, of course, would be unrealistic. For instance, farmers buy gas for their tractors. There are other items they buy for their production process, on which they pay some kind of sales tax or excise tax. Fine. And these taxes are part of the price we ultimately pay for the end product.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the tax burden on food today is perhaps 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent, certainly not more than
Supply
that. And now the Minister and his Government want to increase that burden to as much as 8 per cent, 9 per cent or 10 per cent. We don't know exactly how much. There is a big difference, Mr. Speaker, between a minor tax that indirectly enters into the price of a product and a tax deliberately levied by the Government.
So what is the NDP saying?
We are saying that we should not rely more on indirect taxes. We are saying you should not tax food. We are saying, yes, you should reform the manufacturers' sales tax. We accept the need to broaden the base, Mr. Speaker. We are suggesting that with all of the brain power in the Department of Finance the Department should have been able to do better than what it has done so far. Is the Minister in favour of taxing food? Yes or no? What is the position of the Government?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the questions from the Hon. Member. I would point out that when we went across the country with Tax Probe 86-and I am glad the Member has taken note of that because I think we did do a good job in talking to a broad range of Canadians-what people said most of all was, "Yes, as taxpayers we are prepared to pay our share of federal taxes." We did not find a widespread tax revolt with people saying, "No, the tax burden is so awful, let us cut it by half'. It was not a Proposition 13 type of mentality such as that found in the State of California. What we found instead though was people saying, "When we pay our taxes, we want to know that the tax system is really being just and fair".
One of the things which the Hon. Member's Government has done, which I think has done more than any other single measure to undermine people's confidence in the justice and fairness of the tax system, was to give a half a million dollar exemption on capital gains. We know that 90 per cent of that benefit will go to people in the top 1 per cent or 2 per cent of the income range, to high-flyers speculating in art, land, and whatever else. That is where most of the benefit of that measure has gone. That is why that kind of measure has to be taken away.
An NDP Government would be committed to tax reform along the kinds of principles that I have outlined in a number of speeches both in the House of Commons and elsewhere. We do want to maintain a substantial reliance on direct taxation. We believe that the corporate share of the tax burden in Canada has been allowed to go down too far, both by Liberal and Conservative Governments.
We deplore the degree to which this Government, now in office since 1984, has loaded billions of dollars of additional tax burden on to average Canadians while putting peanut-sized tax demands on the corporate sector. Those are some of the guidelines and principles that we would follow. We believe that if we can get the economy of Canada going, that in itself would reduce government expenditures, increase revenues and

make a major contribution to bringing down the deficit, which I think most people feel is, in the long term, unduly high.

Mr. Speaker, before beginning my remarks, I should like to tell the Hon. Member that the whole question of sales tax on food and other matters will be properly discussed on June 18. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has made that clear, and I ask the Hon. Member to wait until then. He can certainly warn the Government, if that is what he wants to do, and prod the Government not to do things; that is an historic role of the Opposition. However, it is also an historic role of the Opposition-and I want to make this point very clear before I begin my remarks-to present credible alternatives.
In my view the role of the Opposition is to check the Government, to prod the Government, and to be a responsible alternative. What we are hearing this morning is a little of the first and the second and none of the third.
In order for the country to be properly informed in a debate about tax reform, it seems to me that we should have contesting alternatives in the Chamber, not simply negative criticisms of attempts to be constructive in reforming our tax system.
I welcome the opportunity to speak in the debate today and to deal with some of the broad questions on tax reform. The Hon. Member said that he was concerned that the Minister of Finance has not been as informative as he would like. Let me summarize where the Government is, up until now, and set the stage for June 18.
In responding to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), I should note at the start that the timing of his motion is a little strange. In just three weeks from today the Minister of Finance will be presenting to the House and to the country the Government's proposals for tax reform. That is really the time to have this debate, but for some peculiar reason we are having it today. I could have understood why we are having it today if, as I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre had a whole set of alternative proposals to bring to us from his task force and wanted to put them before the House to allow us to criticize and examine them. However, that is not the case. Instead, we hear nothing about that; we just hear warnings about particular fears he has about what might be announced on June 18.
It is bizarre that we are having the debate today but, now that we are having it, let me proceed. The Minister of Finance has already made it clear that important and broad-reaching changes to our tax system will be proposed. He has indicated the general nature of some of the approaches of tax reform. It is clear from this that the White Paper will contain major reforms.
The Hon. Member opposite is clearly impatient. I have already heard his impatience this morning. He is not prepared to wait until June 18 to see exactly what will be proposed, but he will have to wait. Moreover, he has presented a motion with
May 28, 1987

a strangely narrow focus. It ignores the whole broad range of tax issues which have a bearing on the fairness and balance of our tax system.
It is often said that it is good politics to concentrate on one issue and criticize it. I am not too sure that that is what the Canadian public is expecting-just criticism on one aspect of tax reform. I think it is looking for comprehensive reform and it is looking to all Parties not to have a strangely narrow focus but to have a comprehensive focus.
Perhaps it is not so surprising that the motion is couched narrowly, in view of the fact that the Minister of Finance has made the broad directions of tax reform quite clear. It is apparent from what he has said already that a fairer tax system is emerging.
The tax burden will be redistributed, to be shared more equitably among taxpayers in similar circumstances. The Minister has stated that the Government's revenue sources will be better balanced with less reliance on personal income taxes and higher take-home pay for the great majority of Canadians.
I have heard the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) speak on tax reform in the House. His principle seems to be close to but not nearly as specific as that of the Government. However, these principles are supported by Canadians-that we should redistribute the burden, share it more equitably, make the system simpler, and have less reliance on personal income taxes than we have had in the past.
[ Translation]
The Minister has stated that the income tax system for individuals will be improved as a result of reduced tax rates, fewer income tax brackets, fewer special privileges which mainly benefit high income taxpayers and an increased use of tax credits as opposed to tax exemptions, a change that will help very substantially those in the lowest income bracket.
In addition, the switch to a tax credit system may be seen as a progressive social change, because doing so, we can use the personal income tax system to continue to improve the situation of low-income Canadians.

The Minister of Finance has left no doubt about his intentions in this regard. They are changes that will be widely welcomed by Canadians, so it should not be surprising that an opposition motion attacking the Government is silent on all these very positive measures. It is silent, too, on the Minister's stated intention to change the corporate tax system. The corporate tax base will be broadened by eliminating many special preferences and reducing others.
The Hon. Member spoke briefly about corporate tax, but he did not say very much about it. The corporate tax base will be broadened by eliminating many special preferences and reducing others. Many more profitable corporations will pay tax. The resulting increase in revenues will permit a reduction in corporate tax rates, so that they remain competitive with
Supply
those of our major trading partners. Nothing could be more clear about where we are heading with tax reform, which is to lower the rates and broaden the base.
We have not heard much about what Hon. Members opposite would do to bring about improvements which are so badly needed in our sales tax system. The flaws in the sales tax system have been known for many years and documented in a whole series of studies. As a matter of fact, the Hon. Member presented our case when he said that two-thirds of the goods and services in Canada are not taxed, and that we must have a reform of the federal sales tax. I listened closely, and I could not get what his reform of federal sales tax would be. In fact, I asked him direct questions on this and I still could not get the answer.
We have a sales tax which discriminates against our own producers in favour of foreign competitors. This is unbelievable. Any foreigner who looks at our federal sales tax system finds it hard to believe that we would have such a system.
Due to a different tax base, the effective rate of taxes on average is one-third higher on Canadian products. What would Hon. Members opposite do about that? Not only that, but the tax discriminates against similar products made by competing manufacturers within a particular industry. It even discriminates within an industry, as well as discriminating against our exporters.
About one-half of the total sales tax collected is derived from tax on business inputs. The result is an indirect charge on exported goods estimated at about 1 per cent of the sales value of exports, burdening Canadian producers with a competitive disadvantage in world markets. Moreover, the federal sales tax is too narrowly based, as I have said. With such a narrow base, tax rates have been forced to rise for fiscal purposes. The result has been to distort efficient operations in our economy.

speechtext:
This Government made it a reality, and whatever changes will be made to the sales tax must be considered and judged in the over-all context of the tax reform package that will be tabled on June 18.
As I have already mentioned, the Minister of Finance has made it clear that important changes to personal income tax will have a major effect on providing fair tax treatment for lower-income Canadians. Of all the fears I have heard from the Hon. Member opposite, he has totally neglected to mention how the Minister of Finance has made it clear that lower-income Canadians will find their taxes much lower. That was not part of his speech in any way. I can only urge Hon. Members and Canadians generally to judge what we do on its over-all effect on creating a better and fairer federal tax system for Canada.
I would also like to remind the House that the goal of a better and fairer tax system is not a newly adopted policy of the Government. It has been a major priority ever since the Government took office in 1984. In his agenda paper of the fall
of 1984, the Minister of Finance identified the tax system itself as an obstacle to the country's economic growth. I do not know if Canadians realize how important that statement is. There are many obstacles to growth in Canada, but who would have dreamed that the tax system itself was one of those obstacles? It is, and the Minister recognized reform of the tax system as an important aspect of economic renewal.
Since then, in a deliberate and measured way, the Government has introduced a number of important improvements to the tax system. With his first Budget, the Minister of Finance tabled a discussion paper outlining directions for reforming the corporate income tax system and the first phase of those reforms was carried forward in the February, 1986, Budget. We are already in the process of reform and of broadening the tax base to permit a reduction in corporate tax rates. The second phase of corporate tax reform will be launched in the June 18 White Paper.
What has happened already in the area of personal income tax? The tax base has been broadened by the Government by eliminating a number of tax-avoidance and deferral techniques. Not once do we hear anything about that from the Opposition. There are a number of major steps that have already been taken to reduce tax preferences in the corporate sector and in the personal income sector. We have eliminated a number of tax-avoidance and deferral techniques-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext: And created new ones.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext:
I would be very happy to go through examples of those during Question Period. What we have created that is new is a minimum tax to ensure that high-income earners cannot avoid paying any tax. We never hear about that either. As well, the first steps were taken toward finding a replacement for the inadequate federal sales tax. A review was undertaken of selected social and tax transfer programs.
There is much to be said about how far the Government has already gone on tax reform before the statement of June 18. It soon became apparent, however, that if we were to achieve our goals of tax reform, we would have to undertake a major restructuring of personal income tax as well. That led to the announcement last July of the Government's intention to proceed with comprehensive tax reform. The goals and guidelines of tax reform were set out by the Minister of Finance in the Blue Book he tabled in the House on October 23.
Fairness is the key measure of tax reform. The tax system must ensure a fair sharing of the tax burden. People in similar circumstances are not now treated equally. They will be treated equally after tax reform. High-income earners and profitable corporations should pay their fair share of taxes and similar products should bear the same rate of sales tax. The previous Government felt that it could not act on any of these but we will act on them.
The tax system should also be simpler so Canadians may understand it and comply with it. I recall that two or three
May 28, 1987

months ago, I met with the Chinese Minister of Trade who asked me what the books were that were sitting in the corner of the Department of Finance boardroom. I said that they were interpretation bulletins and the Statutes of the Canadian Income Tax Act, comprising about 3,000 pages. I asked how big the Chinese income tax document was, and he said that it was six pages. I do not think we will ever be able to get that much simplicity, but Canadians want a simpler system, a system that will allow them to understand and to do their income tax returns themselves. That is a major motive behind the reforms we will be bringing in on June 18.
Another important objective has been to achieve a better balance of federal revenue sources with less reliance on personal income tax. We also seek greater stability and certainty in federal revenues. There are other important concerns which help shape tax reform, including the need to encourage economic growth and to remove distortions in business decision-making created by tax incentives, the need to reinforce international competitiveness and the need to reflect Canada's social and economic priorities.
We have been concerned that any tax changes should be implemented with appropriate provisions for transition to the new tax system. I think it is important that we signal that now. Throughout we have consulted broadly with Canadians in developing the proposals we have submitted to the House. Consultation is important. The last time there was a major effort at tax reform in the MacEachen Budget, there was not appropriate consultation. The Government was caught unawares time and time again and in a humiliating way had to change at least 49 major parts of that Budget.
We have been consulting. In fact, in order to minimize surprises, we have also brought forward papers for debate and discussion. The Hon. Member could not have introduced this motion and debated it in the way he has if the subject had not been raised by the Government. He wants to talk only about food, but all the other aspects that he does not discuss have been in the public domain. Canadians understand them and that will help in the understanding of tax reform when we table our major document on June 18.
I am confident that the White Paper will be judged a success in meeting those guidelines. I think the consultations we have already undertaken will have been very helpful. I was told that in New Zealand, there was a government information office on the sales tax system and it was able to be closed before the tax was even brought in because the people of New Zealand were so well informed about what the Government was doing.
I think consultation has helped set the stage for the Canadian people to sympathize with and understand what we intend to do. In particular, I am sure that impartial judges will conclude that tax reform meets its central objective, which is to reduce tax rates. Mr. Speaker, I know it is the duty of the Opposition to express skepticism. However, to express skepticism in the midst of concrete actions in the opposite direction is less understandable. Let us look at the tax fairness measures which we have implemented to date. The proof is in what we have done since 1984.
We ended the scientific research tax credit abuse which was terribly expensive. We eliminated tax shelters based on investment in yachts, recreational vehicles and similar properties. We eliminated the Registered Home Ownership Savings Program. We brought about the elimination of income splitting among family members by using interest-free loans in order to minimize tax. We imposed a minimum tax on high income individuals, which is something the Hon. Member called for.
From July to December, 1985, actions were taken to stop the so-called carve-out transactions in the oil and gas sector and to prevent the use of trusts through market securities issued in such a way that income and capital returns to investors were distributed tax free. We ended the use of partnership and corporate takeovers to increase tax deductions through the so-called partnership step-up rules. The list goes on. All of these measures are evidence that reform is under way.
In addition, the Government is committed to replacing exemptions with credits. This is a very, very progressive move. In the 1987 Budget the Government indicated that it would do this. In addition, through the federal sales tax credit and the child tax credit we have already given concrete evidence that we are moving in this direction.
Exemptions favour those in the higher tax brackets, and I do not know why Hon. Members do not mention this. Each $1,000 of exemption is worth $60 in federal sales tax saving to a lower income individual in the 6 per cent tax bracket, while it is worth $340 to a person in the top 34 per cent tax bracket. Credits provide the same amount of tax reduction to taxpayers at all income levels. That is why it is so important to move to a credit system. Finally, moving to credits will mean more benefits for lower income taxpayers and less for those at higher income levels.
I do not ask the Opposition to cease being skeptical. That is the job of the Opposition. However, I do ask Members to look at these concrete, progressive moves which show that we are

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe my ears. I cannot believe that the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) said in his speech that the tax credit which is currently given to families is used to buy food. That tax credit was originally instituted by previous Liberal Governments to help those poor families that could not afford to buy clothing, furniture, or some of the big ticket items. It was certainly never intended to pay for food.
That mentality of the Minister is an indication of what we can expect on June 18. We already hear the Minister saying "sales tax credit to pay for food". Shame on the Government, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State for Finance who claim that they will bring in tax reform. They will bring in tax reform all right. Just ask low-income Canadians including senior citizens living below the poverty line on pensions what kind of tax they are now paying as a result of the Government's so-called reforms instituted in the November Economic Statement in a cumulative way.
Does the Minister really think the Canadian people are that stupid? Does he really think they cannot read the taxes they are now paying in the low and middle-income brackets as a result of the changes made by the Government which favour the rich? We heard the Minister expound on how fair tax credits were as compared with exemptions. He did not mention the $.5 million capital gains exemption which he and his friends on Bay Street have offered to the top 2 per cent of the population which can afford to earn such capital gains.
In the last two and a half years the Government has wreaked a tax expense havoc on the poor and middle-income families which has been unprecedented in Canadian history. We now see the ultimate blow in the form of a tax on food. We heard the Minister of State for Finance talk about what happened when the wonderful socialist Government in New Zealand imposed a 10 per cent tax on food. Yes, in the shortterm they saw their take-home pay increase because their income tax had been reduced. However, they also saw prices increase dramatically.
In the first three months following the imposition of a 10 per cent tax on food the Consumer Price Index increased by 8.9 per cent. The Minister said that he could not foresee an increase in the CPI. That is because he has not studied the issue. He has not looked at what has happened in other jurisdictions. It is quite clear that there will be an increase in inflation. It is quite clear that a tax on bread and milk will hit those who can least afford to pay.
We could not pin the Minister down today on exactly what the Government intends to do on June 18, but we heard a bit of the line, the Dalton Camp line, which is probably being crafted now in the Office of the Prime Minister. God forbid that the Government should get itself in the same kind of a mess with the food tax as it got itself in on its attempt to cut back on senior citizens' pensions. I am sure the Government

will have a finely honed, finely crafted line, part of which we heard today from the Minister of State for Finance.
He said that the Government will broaden the base. A food tax will certainly broaden the base. Instead of taxing luxury items and other specific items as is currently the case under federal sales tax legislation, we will be taxing milk, bread, and other food when we already know from looking at the figures for the last 20 years that Canadians are already paying more to eat and survive than for lodging.
A recent article in Maclean's magazine gives a fairly good picture of how hard Canadians are already being hit for the cost of food. Between 1961 and 1986 Canadians have increased the amount of money they pay for food up to 25 per cent. The amount they pay for shelter has increased by 19 per cent and the amount they pay for taxes has increased by over 33.5 per cent on average. We can see that the amount spent for food has increased tremendously, and yet the Government is going to add a double-whammy if it introduces a tax on food on June 18. Will the Government that was elected with the largest majority in our history receive the support of Canadians to tax food? No. Nearly two out of every three Canadians oppose the Government's proposal to extend federal sales tax to cover food and services.
Food is not the only item. Food is a very basic item, but will we see the Government introduce a tax on day care? Will we see it introduce a tax on other essential services at the same time that it claims it will introduce these other beneficial measures for working families?
The Government claims that it will broaden the tax base and introduce a fairer system. Yet it is really introducing a tax grab for the federal Treasury. The Government likely receives its advice from Deloitte, Haskins and Sells, who suggested just last week that it will be cheaper for the federal Government to tax food and provide a tax credit than not to tax food at all. Deloitte, Haskins and Sells are making preliminary calculations which suggest that it will be cheaper for the Government to tax food. The federal Government will be in a position to collect $20 billion if it comes forward with the business transfer tax of 8 per cent. Its tax credits, which it will potentially give only to families earning below $15,000-far below the poverty line in most communities in Canada-would only amount to $3 billion. Therefore, the net gain to the federal Treasury is $17 billion.
While the Government talks about tax fairness, it will literally be taking food out of the mouths of babes if it introduces this food tax that is being suggested in the June 18 financial statement by the Minister.

very quick tenure as Premier of Ontario. One reason why Mr. Miller went down to defeat, apart from the fact that we had an extremely able Premier to take his place, was that as Treasurer in Ontario he introduced a tax on candy, ice cream and chocolate bars for children, as well as a tax on tampons. There are certain elements in Canadian life that are absolutely essential, one of which is food. If the Minister of Finance really believes he can sell Canadians the notion that while imposing a tax across the board on food consumers will receive a somewhat bigger cheque at the end of the year, it is obvious that the Minister of Finance is not the one doing the shopping in his household. He will not be able to convince the senior citizens who, for the first time, are paying taxes as a result of the regressive tax policies of the Government. It is also obvious that the Minister of State for Finance does not balance the budget in his household.
Canadians pay for their food on a weekly basis and must pay for it with cash. The figures from Deloitte, Haskins and Sells are selfexplanatory and indicate that the imposition of a food tax, including the tax credit that may be given, may still result in a net benefit to the federal Treasury of a billion dollars more than what it would be without the food tax. Most of those children come from one-parent homes led by mothers. These families cannot afford to pay a tax on food, nor can middle-

income families afford a tax on food as a result of the cumulative tax policy since 1984, as part of the so-called tax reform package introduced by that great reformer. Leonard Shifrin, a social policy analyst, called the Minister the "great deceiver", which 1 believe is a perfect name.
A family of four with both parents working, earning $35,000 a year, which represents a fairly average family in certain areas of the country, will be paying over the life of the tax reform package an extra $3,452 through increases in income taxes as well as losses through the cut-back in family allowances.
These average families are gouged by almost 10 per cent of their gross income in a tax period of three to four years. The Minister will then return to the House on June 18 and say that he will offer them a tax break and broaden the base. That was the catch phrase used by the Minister of State this morning which, in simple English, means taxing everything that Canadians use. It may even include such areas of service as daycare and medicare. The enormity of the tax grab on middle and lower-income Canadians as a result of the Government's potential initiatives on June 18 is so devastating that I cannot even begin to describe it.

Mr. Speaker, we know that the Minister of State himself revealed the kind of attitude he has towards poorer people when he said, among other things: We, the Government, pay the sales tax, we pay the sales tax credit to poorer families so they will be able to eat. But when the tax credits were introduced by former Liberal Government a few years ago, it was not for food, it was to give families an opportunity to buy various things such as clothes and big ticket items. This is why we came up with the tax credit, not to pay for food. Indeed we can already guess that the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) with his colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have begun to toy with the idea of taxing food.
We can only recall the situation in New Zealand where a socialist Government imposed a 10 per cent tax. Even the New Democratic Party . . . Here in Canada we have precious little opportunity to examine the Government performance because it does not perform all that much. However, we have the example of New Zealand, and I was rather surprised to hear the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), who strongly criticized the Conservative Government, reply to my question about what he thought of the action taken by the Socialist Government in New Zealand: "That is not the same. The Socialist Government in New Zealand imposed a 10 per cent tax on food products, which caused an 8.9 per cent, or nearly 9 per cent increase in the cost of living over the next three-month period. And who is affected by a higher cost of living index? The poor, the old, the underprivileged. Someone with a $100,000 income will not lose any sleep if the cost of

living index goes up by 7 per cent or 8 per cent. However, someone who spends the larger part of his income on food and housing does.
During the last 20 years, the percentage of average income paid by Canadians on food alone has increased to 25 per cent. Food has become even more expensive than housing in Canada. We already spend 25 per cent of our average income to eat. The so-called tax reform of the Minister, which will supposedly be clarified on June 18, will involve additional taxes, and a tax on food products is even being considered.
A former Ontario Premier tried it before. He imposed a tax on candy, or a kiddy tax, such as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has himself imposed this year. However, the tax on food products and the possible tax on day-care, in view of the need for such services, represent taxes on the necessities of life. There are no two ways about it. People have to eat. There are Canadians who have to rely on a steady diet of macaroni, and sometimes even cat food. There occasionally are articles in newspapers describing the plight of the poor. If we look at the so-called tax reforms brought in after the 1984 Budget, we find, for instance, that a family with a $15,000 annual income, which is certainly not astronomical, has already lost a total of $1,844 in the three years this Government has been in power. subtopic: SANCTUARY SOUGHT FOR GRIZZLY BEARS IN KHUTZEYMATEEN VALLEY
SANCTUARY SOUGHT FOR GRIZZLY BEARS IN KHUTZEYMATEEN VALLEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the arrival of the white man, the grizzly bear has been driven from over half of its natural habitat in North America. Highly sensitive to human activity, the grizzly now only exists in significant numbers in areas of British Columbia, Alberta, Yukon, Northwest Territories, and Alaska. Despite this alarming decline, Canada does not have a single sanctuary dedicated primarily to the protection of the grizzly.
The best candidate for such a sanctuary is the Khut-zeymateen Valley north of Prince Rupert on the B.C. coast. Khutzeymateen is one of the last undisturbed valleys on the West Coast. The Khutzeymateen has been recognized by the United Nations as a globally unique and significant site. Most important, the Khutzeymateen has one of the highest concentrations of grizzly bears left in Canada. The Khutzeymateen would be an excellent choice as Canada's first grizzly bear sanctuary.
Unfortunately, the Khutzeymateen, like so many other ecologically important areas in B.C., is threatened by logging. This would be a terrible mistake that would only further reduce the grizzly's already shrinking habitat and population.
I call upon the Government to take the initiative and begin immediate negotiations with the Government of British Columbia to establish a grizzly bear sanctuary in the Khutzeymateen Valley.

subtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-COMPENSATION ISSUE
INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-COMPENSATION ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hopes that the Government would achieve an honourable redress for Japanese-Canadian dispossession during World War II seem very near being blasted entirely. One Minister's promise of negotiations two and a half years ago did not survive the second meeting with the National Association of Japanese Canadians. A second Minister's promise of a fair, equitable and honourable resolution was never given any practical expression. A third Minister's promise to obtain approval for a process of negotiation has ended in a take-it-or-forget-it ultimatum from his Chief of Staff.
Forty-five years ago a Liberal Government yielded to racial prejudice in British Columbia and disrupted a peaceable community. Today a Conservative Government refuses to find the financial resources required to do the honourable thing by redressing individuals.
The Government has never really negotiated with the NAJC. The hopes of June, 1984, lie in ruins. One more promise has been broken. Clearly it will require a different Government to clear the national honour of this genocidal blot.

Mr. Speaker, the whole House rejoiced with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) when, by persistent effort, he obtained the release of Josyp Terelya, Danylo Shumuk, and others. Mr. Speaker, May 28 is Armenian Independence Day. Between 1918 and 1920 the short-lived independent Republic of Armenia had an impressive record of social democracy. During the first elections in June, 1919, all adults of both sexes, including Muslim and Russian minorities, were granted the right to vote in universal, secret and proportional balloting. Six political Parties participated and 80 members were elected, among whom were women and representatives of the minorities.
Despite the extended pressures building against the Republic and the internal problems of hunger, disease and poverty, this tiny nation founded a university, provided schools for Muslim minorities, and authorized formation of labour unions. Courts were established and the jury system was introduced for the first time in that area of the world.
Certainly it was the commitment of the Armenian people to democracy and social welfare, in addition to their past sufferings, that led the Government of Canada, on April 1, 1920, to place itself formally on record as absolutely opposed to the return of any Armenian provinces of Turkey to Turkish rule.

Mr. Speaker, I was delighted with the copyright Bill tabled yesterday. These amendments are just the first step in a comprehensive revision of the Act. A second Bill dealing with other copyright issues will be tabled in the House as soon as possible, probably in the fall.
The abolition of the compulsory licensing of sound recordings is most welcome. By abolishing this provision, a grave restriction on musical copyright will be removed. The composer of a song or the copyright owner will be freely able to negotiate fees and conditions through the market-place.
This new Bill encourages the creation of new types of collectives in all areas of copyright. It also expands creator's moral rights.
The Bill introduces a new right, that of exhibition. Artists will now have a right over the public exhibition of their work.
I trust that the second set of revisions to be tabled will address the issue of classroom use of copyright material, an issue I brought up in the House late last fall. The Bill tabled yesterday is very encouraging for all Canadians directly or indirectly involved in matters relating to copyright. I look forward to step two.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have never seen such a display of ignorance in this House.
The judicial power in the United States has the same independence that our Canadian institutions provide for our judicial power. And why should it be otherwise? When a Canadian judicial body makes a decision contrary to the will of U.S. citizens, that is the responsibility of the body in question, and the Government of Canada is not asked to reverse a judicial decision. That is what we call division of powers.
To infer that we can, at will, blur those divisions between the judicial, legislative and executive powers is erroneous in the extreme, Mr. Speaker.
As for the question of Investment Canada, the Hon. Member knows perfectly well, and if he didn't, he does now, because I can inform him no such requests were made.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. His colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, has just stated that the Government knew that this was a quasijudicial process and that there was no power of intervention. If that is the case, why did the Prime Minister, with full knowledge of that, then undertake to write the letter to President Reagan holding out the hope to the western Canadian oil and gas industry that he was personally going to do something about it? Why were that expectation and hope raised when the Government already knew it was bound to fail?
