Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. the Prime Minister who received last week an invitation from the leaders of aboriginal organizations to meet with them here in Ottawa during this week's conference to discuss the implications of the Meech Lake accord over which they entertain serious and legitimate concerns.
Is the Prime Minister prepared to meet with the leaders of the main aboriginal organizations at the earliest opportunity to set up a negotiation program to complete the Canadian Confederation by including the aboriginal peoples' right to self-government?

subsubtopic: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES' RIGHTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for this question. Indeed, on four occasions, through constitutional conferences on aboriginal issues, we attempted to reintegrate, to give native peoples the full benefit of Canada's constitutional provisions.
Again recently, despite our best efforts, we as a nation failed in this latest attempt. I pointed out at the time, and again here in the House, that in spite of that failure-my friend would know that the provinces must co-operate if we are to succeed- at the appropriate time I would of course be prepared to reopen the case and make a new attempt to propose a fair integration process to the native peoples with respect to the Canadian Constitution.
I remain available and interested in seeing this process through to its successful completion.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all Canadians appreciate the Prime Minister's commitment. What concrete measures will he take to ensure that a schedule is set up for negotiations to include aboriginal selfgovernment rights in the Constitution, and will he raise this matter with the Premiers at the next meeting?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: METHOD OF PRESENTATION OF PETITIONS-MR. SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lewis) has been patiently awaiting, for quite some time, the Chair's comments on a matter which he raised on March 23 last. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, on a point of order, questioned the current practice with respect to the presentation of petitions. In particular, he pointed out a number of instances where petitions were certified by the Clerk of Petitions and then presented to the House some weeks or months later. He claimed that a lengthy lapse of time between the certification of a petition and its presentation in the House denied those Canadians who were petitioning the opportunity for speedy redress of their grievances. It also, he claimed, denied the Government the right to reply promptly.
So that all Hon. Members and the public will understand, under the rules of this place when a petition is presented either by an Hon. Member rising to his or her feet to present it, or by filing it at the Table, the Government is now required under the rules to reply to that petition in so many days. It is important that all Hon. Members and the public which is watching this understand that because that is a key ingredient of these remarks.
The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary is raising an extremely legitimate complaint here. Any Canadian who signs a petition would not expect that several months would elapse from the date the petition is first signed until a response is forthcoming. While a delay of several weeks is potentially required in order to allow for the collection of signatures, the transmittal to Ottawa, the certification by the Clerk of Petitions, the presentation in the House, and the response by the Government, most Canadians would agree that delays of some seven or eight months, as pointed out by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, are difficult to justify.
The second point raised by the Parliamentary Secretary dealt with the presentation of petitions by Members other than the Member who had the petition certified. As Hon. Members will know, before a petition can be presented it must be certified at the Table. He claimed that this practice would be misleading because when Members from across the country were presenting petitions the implication could be drawn that a particular issue was of more widespread concern to Canadians than possibly was the case.

By way of response to these two points let me first quote Standing Order 106(1) which states:
Prior to presentation, the Clerk of Petitions shall examine all petitions, and in
order to be presented, they must be certified correct as to form and content by
the said Clerk.
There is no specific mention in this Standing Order of any requirement to present a petition within a specific time frame, only the point that "prior to presentation" it must be certified.
May 28, 1987

The Chair consulted the McGrath Committee report of June 1985 which recommended this particular Standing Order to see whether any indication was given there of a possible restriction on the period of time between certification and presentation but could find no guidance.

To take the matter further, in Beauchesne's Fifth Edition Citation 691 states:
A Member cannot be compelled to present a petition. In a subsequent action, it was held that there is no right in a person desirous of petitioning the House to compel any Member to present his petition and that no action will lie against a Member for refusing to do so.
If there is no requirement that a Member present a petition, can there be a requirement that a petition should be presented within a specified period of time following certification? On March 23, 1987, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) ably pointed out that various reasons might prevent a Member from presenting a certified petition expeditiously. I would suggest to Members that several months need not elapse between certification and presentation in most circumstances. However, I agree with the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) that the present Standing Order does not impose any specific restriction.

To address the second point raised by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary let me quote Standing Order 106(4) which states:
Any Member desiring to present a petition in his or her place in the House may do so on "Presenting Petitions-"
There is no specific mention here that the Member presenting the petition must be the Member who had it certified, or indeed that it must be the Member in whose riding the petitioners reside. There is no restriction stated in the Standing Order. It merely states "any member".
On a careful reading of the Standing Orders and a strict interpretation of those Standing Orders, I can find no requirement that the Member who has the petition certified must be the Member who presents it. In fact, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier pointed out, Beauchesne's Citations 689 and 690 specifically relate to Members presenting petitions for other Members.
However, because the current Standing Orders relating to petitions are provisional and have only been in force for a short time, and because the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure is in the process of considering the Standing Orders at the present time, it might be timely to suggest to members of this committee that they may wish to pay particular attention to the Standing Orders relating to the presentation of petitions, if as the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary has contended, these particular Standing Orders are causing concern.
Supply
As these provisional Standing Orders are now written, I am unable to order that the Member who has a petition certified be the same Member who presents it to the House, nor can I define any time restriction for the period between the certification and the presentation of a petition.
I do, however, feel that the issues raised by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, are legitimate ones dealing with the fundamental right of every citizen to petition the House of Commons and to expect speedy redress. I would suggest to all Members that they give this issue their close attention. I thank Hon. Members for their representations.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Cassidy:
That this House oppose any imposition of a federal tax on food and urge the Government to reject any such tax as part of its tax reform package.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are debating a motion by the New Democratic Party which expresses the view of hundreds of thousands of Canadians who do not want the sales tax extended, and certainly do not want it applied to food.
This country has been governed by Liberal Governments for 50 of the last 60 years. During those years the tax system became increasingly unfair. In the last year for which we have figures, over 200 Canadians with incomes of $250,000 or more paid no income tax. Many of the most profitable corporations in this country have paid no corporation taxes for years. Indeed, there is the recent example of the Gulf Canada purchase in which the purchasers were able to avoid payment of $500 million in corporation taxes which they should have paid.
We realize today that we mistakenly believed the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) during the last election campaign to be sincere when he said he believed in a more fair and equitable tax system. Unfortunately, the record proves the exact opposite. Since the Government has been in office it has loaded increased taxes on ordinary citizens and has made it easier for those in the high income brackets and those wealthy corporations to pay even less than they did in the past.
On May 6, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) condemned the current sales tax regime as being flawed and inadequate. We agree with that. However, he went on to say that he wanted to replace the sales tax system with "a broad-based, multi-stage sales tax". This concept can mean virtually anything. It could mean that there will be a tax on almost all goods and services at all stages of production and development

May 28, 1987
Supply
of consumption items. It could mean that there will be a tax on everyday transactions such as a tenant paying rent, a parent taking a child to day care, or someone visiting a dentist. The Government has been very careful not to make public the details of what it proposes.
We have estimated that the average Canadian family spends about $5,000 a year on food. Under a new Conservative sales tax regime, the average Canadian family might pay a minimum of $300 in new taxes if food is not exempted from this new tax. We intend to fight such a proposal if and when the Government attempts to bring it forward. The Government has argued that it will minimize the difficulties which will be created for low and middle-income people by this new sales tax through the use of an enhanced refundable sales tax credit which, at the present time, gives adults $50 in refunds and children $25 in refunds. However, the National Council of Welfare has calculated that while this form of tax relief does reduce the sales tax burden considerably, it does not fully offset the cost of recent Conservative sales and excise tax increases. Furthermore, the tax credit is only available to families with incomes between $10,000 and $15,000.
We have made some calculations on what tax increases have meant to ordinary Canadian families since the Conservative Government took office. As a result of the November, 1985 economic statement of the Minister of Finance, there were increases in oil and gas price, unemployment insurance premiums, and an increase in sales tax. That cost the ordinary family $425.
The May, 1985 Budget eliminated the federal tax reduction, modified indexing of income tax, cut the family allowance payments, broadened the sales tax base, increased cigarettes and alcohol tax, and increased the gas tax. That cost the ordinary family $512 in the course of a year.
There were further increases in the Budget of February 26, 1986. There was a 3 per cent surtax on income tax, a sales tax increase, and an increase in taxes for cigarettes and alcohol. That cost the family $340 in a year.
In February of this year there were further increases in the gas tax. The sales tax base was broadened and cigarette and air ticket taxes were increased. That cost the family about $80.
The cost to the ordinary family of increases in taxes by the Conservative Government has been $1,384 in the course of a year.
The New Democratic Party and the National Council on Welfare are not the only ones to criticize the imposition of a business transfer tax. Mr. Bulloch's Canadian Federation of Independent Business, whose membership includes tens of thousands of small-business people, have opposed such a tax.
The Minister of Finance has said that one of the chief objectives of tax reform is to give the majority of Canadians more take home pay by way of a personal tax cut. We are concerned that what the Conservatives give with one hand they
will just as likely take with the other through increases, hidden sales taxes.
This is not only true of sales taxes. We have seen a steady increase in the use of consumption taxes. We oppose the increased use of consumption taxes because we believe that it is regressive and shifts corporate tax burdens directly on to consumers. We believe that not only do corporations not pay their fair share, they pass their share of taxes on to consumers.
The increased use of sales taxes is a blow to the fair and progressive tax system in Canada that was almost destroyed by former Liberal Governments. Yet this is exactly the direction in which the Conservative tax changes have taken us since 1984.

As a consequence of the last three Budgets, and one economic statement, Canadians are now paying over $20 billion in new sales and excise taxes, or will be by 1990. That amounts to an additional $910 for an average Canadian family over and above what we were paying in sales taxes prior to the time the Conservatives took office. It is also one of the largest single tax increases in Canadian history.
What this has meant in terms of how the Government gets its revenue can be explained very simply. The revenue that personal income taxes have brought to the Government has increased by 43 per cent. The revenue which came to the Government as a result of the increases it instituted through indirect taxes has increased by 56 per cent. The revenue of the Government from changes in the corporate income tax has increased by just three-tenths of 1 per cent. So it is pretty obvious to us who the Conservative Government represents.
We believe in a fair and progressive tax system, a system where individual incomes above a basic level are taxed on a progressive and graduated basis in order to redistribute the income from the wealthy to average and lower income Canadians and to achieve a more equal society. The past and future addiction of the Conservatives to sales tax increases will mean a serious erosion of progressivity in the tax system as consumption taxes take up an increasingly higher proportion of over-all revenues.
In 1986 alone, sales tax increases managed to move the percentage of revenues represented by these taxes from 22.3 per cent to much more. Tax reform proposals which the Minister will bring in in a few weeks will undoubtedly propel this percentage higher. It is the equivalent of imposing a flat tax on all incomes regardless of whether the person is rich or poor.
Let us deal with what a tax on food will do. It is important to note that the Conservatives have already put in motion their methods of collecting sales tax on food. In February of this year they extended the federal sales tax to snack foods effective July 1. A month from now we are going to see the kids paying more for their potato chips and chocolate bars.
May 28, 1987

This tax will primarily hit children and raise $120 million in revenue. It will cost the average family about $15 a year.
Why would a Government which cares about the Canadian people impose that kind of tax when it lets the purchasers of Gulf Canada avoid paying $500 million in taxes? If the Government had collected that tax which the purchasers should have paid, and were obligated to pay by law, except for the very strange ruling by Revenue Canada, the Government would not have to do most of the things it is doing.
We have estimated that the average Canadian family will pay $300 in new taxes as a result of taxing food. That is if the new tax is what is called "revenue neutral", in other words, if it is set at 6 per cent. However, what is to prevent the present Conservative Government, which is so concerned about the deficit, from setting the rate not at 6 per cent but at 7 per cent or 8 per cent or higher, as it is in many European countries? This would mean an increased cost of about $350 or $400 a year to the average family.
We say that tax increases on such fundamental living items will generate a tax revolt among Canadians. The people of Canada took the Prime Minister seriously when he talked before the election about a fairer, simpler, less complex tax system. He said that Canadians who were wealthy and corporations which were profitable would pay their fair share of taxes. We are still waiting for that. We are certain that the imposition of a tax on food is precisely the wrong way in which the people of Canada want this Government, or any government, to go. Therefore, we give notice now that we will fight such a proposal if it is in the White Paper the Minister will be bringing down shortly. We will fight it with everything we have, both in Parliament and outside of this place among the ordinary people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, what I said today and what we have always said is that we believe that the services the people of Canada want and need have to be paid for in one way or another, but we also believe that the tax system should be as fair as possible. That is why we are opposed to increases in hidden taxes. That is why we are opposed to increases in sales taxes, the business-transfer tax or value-added tax, whatever name or label one wants to give to that kind of tax. We are opposed to any increases. We believe that the loopholes in the income tax should be plugged so that everyone will have to pay a fair share. Why should a teller in a bank pay more in income tax than the bank he works for pays in corporation taxes? Why

should a clerk at the Hudson Bay store pay more in income tax than the Hudson Bay Company pays in corporation taxes?
We say we want to plug the holes in the Income Tax Act, most of which were created when the Liberals formed the Government. We want fairness. We want the large corporations to pay taxes at least at the same rate and with the same consistency as the small businessman. There is more than $30 billion in deferred corporation taxes owing, and 90 per cent of that or more is owed by a very small number of the largest corporations.
Are we proposing that all the sales taxes which are already there should be removed? Of course, we cannot do that because we cannot do everything at one time. What we are saying is we do not want any increase or broadening of the sales tax base, and we want those individuals who are wealthy and those corporations which are profitable to pay their fair share of taxes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who is, as I am, a Manitoban. We have in Manitoba a NDP Government, one of two in Canada. I think we can use them as an example of NDP tax policy in action.
On March 16 a Budget was introduced in Manitoba. It increased taxes for four out of every five Manitobans. The retail sales tax was increased. In spite of the Hon. Member's comment that the NDP is opposed to a consumptive tax, the NDP in Manitoba raised the sales tax from 6 per cent to 7 per cent. The Government extended the provincial sales tax to include take-out meals. The payroll tax was increased by 60 per cent. Every small business in Manitoba pays a tax on gross payroll, and that figure was increased by 50 per cent. A 2 per cent tax was imposed on net income for every Manitoban. This basically means a 21 per cent tax increase for a single mother earning $27,000 per year. However, if a taxpayer is part of a childless couple making over $200,000 per year then that couple will pay less than half the increase that a single mother will pay. If there is going to be a tax revolt it will be in Manitoba where we pay the highest rate of provincial tax in the country.
In light of what the Hon. Member has said I am wondering if he and his federal colleagues have passed on their feelings and their displeasure with the Manitoba budget to their cohorts in Manitoba.

He is here to sow fear in the minds of average and ordinary Canadians. His Party was created on fear and it continues to exist on fear. I refer not to the fear of realities but to the fear of myths, the fear of suspicions which the Hon. Member and members of his Party try to sow in the minds of other Canadians.
One thing that is a reality and about which we know is the fact that before the last Budget there was a federal sales tax on certain, what we might describe as, junk foods. The Hon. Member spoke about the extension of the federal sales tax to other junk foods during his remarks.
I have in my riding a company by the name of Wrigley which produces chewing gum. It complained to me and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) about the fact that the federal sales tax prior to the last Budget applied to it but not to its direct competitors which produced potato chips and things of that sort. That was a disadvantage to Wrigley that was
driving it out of business. That was threatening to put its 300 employees, some of whom I suspect were supporters of the Hon. Member's Party, out of work and onto the street. In fact, the last Budget imposed a sales tax which applied fairly to competing products in this area.
Based on what the Hon. Member says I have the impression that he thinks we should do away with sales tax on this type of food. Can he tell us whether or not he would remove the federal sales tax, not only on things such as potato chips, a measure which was included in the last Budget, but also on Wrigley's chewing gum? If that is his position and the position of his Party then will he tell us whether or not the following resolution passed at the 1977 NDP federal convention is still the policy of his Party?
Be it further resolved that a surtax shall be placed on junk foods to make them

Mr. Speaker, let me begin by saying that if the polls showed that the NDP was still at 18 per cent we would not have Conservative Members of Parliament digging out resolutions passed at NDP conventions 10 or more years ago. speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate, after the comments by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), and I hope I will
May 28, 1987

be able to rouse the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), on whom our colleague's comments seemed to have a soporific effect. I think it is important to clarify the Government's intentions with respect to tax reform. Mr. Speaker, you will recall, and I do not want to go back to early 1984, but you will recall that when we were elected, we promised that, as a Government, we would bring in a complete program for economic renewal, and this program included improving the tax system. Mr. Speaker, when we talk about tax reform, we are not talking about your usual budget with a few amendments to the Income Tax Act, as it affects personal income tax and corporate taxes, and some changes in the federal sales tax. We are really talking about the kind of tax reform that will be as important as the last one, which dates back to 1971. Last July, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced his intention of proceeding with a study of the options the Government had for a thorough reform of the Canadian tax system. In October, he identified the specific guidelines for this reform. Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, repeat them here.
First, fairness; second, simplification; third, ease of compliance; fourth, balance; fifth, revenue stability; sixth, international competitiveness; seventh, economic growth; eighth, Canadian priorities; ninth, measured transition; and finally, Mr. Speaker, consultation.
The Minister of Finance is following these 10 guidelines to prepare the tax reform and the White Paper which will be announced on June 18. But why exactly? What do those guidelines mean, Mr. Speaker?
First, I believe that is is essentiel to ensure a fairer distribution of the tax burden so that Canadian taxpayers in comparable circumstances will pay the same amount of taxes. We must also ensure that corporations pay their fair share of taxes. Mr. Speaker, I shall not list the aberrations introduced in our tax system by the former Liberal Government. 1 shall only mention in passing the scientific research tax credit which lost billions of dollars in revenue for the Canadian Government and in assistance those who really needed it.
Mr. Speaker, I shall wait for the questions of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre before replying.
There is another point which should be emphasized. I recall that, when I was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue, the Hon. Perrin Beatty, we said that selfassessment should be maintained and that Canadian taxpayers should work in co-operation with their Government in this regard. However, this does not mean that there is no need to simplify our tax system.
At the same time, we must bring back some balance to the sources of public revenue. In so doing, Mr. Speaker, we must take action to ensure that the tax system will become less dependent on personal income tax and that Canadian taxpayers have more money at their disposal. This is the purpose of our tax reform. Canadians whose taxes were too high will have more money in their pockets. Businesses which took advantage of the unfair benefits granted by the former Government will
Supply
pay a fair and reasonable amount of taxes. At the same time, the Government will have enough money to pursue its economic development initiatives and maintain useful programs. However, in this context, while we speak about our regions, our provinces and our country, we must also remember that Canada must compete with the United States, Japan, France, New Zealand, Australia and Great Britain, many of which are also reforming their own tax system.
Mr. Speaker, our tax system must be just and fair and deal strictly with tax matters; it should not be an income tax legislation dealing with regional development or economic development. Our tax system should help the Canadian economy, but the purpose of our tax legislation should not be regional development. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, that tax reform should help create a positive climate so that the people of Canada, with a little more money in their pockets, should be able to invest at the regional level in your riding, Mr. Speaker, in the Trois-Rivieres constituency, in the constituency of my Hon. colleague, to invest in the Canadian economy and trust that Canadian economy and of course their tax system. Now, Mr. Speaker, those principles are the underlying principles of the tax reform which will be tabled by the Hon. Minister of Finance on June 18.
Opposition Members are against that tax reform. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, and I shall quote-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext: Against the tax reform? But you-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext:
They are against the tax reform. That is what you said, that you were against it. . . I could quote, Mr. Speaker, from some of the suggestions and recommendations of a tax reform committee: "The Canadian tax system should be as close as possible to, but not necessarily a blueprint of, the U.S. tax system, it should increase the corporate tax rate instead of paying specific attention to profit transfers by foreign-based companies, instead of dealing with the appropriateness of a minimum tax calculation for companies, it should be used to establish tighter administrative controls for companies and to tax every source of income whatsoever, it should deal with the $25,000 life insurance tax exemption". I could go on, Mr. Speaker, as there are several more pages of similar suggestions. Mr. Speaker, I have just quoted part of a report submitted to me by a group of businessmen in my riding of Trois-Rivieres: Pierre Bettez, a chartered accountant; Pierre Dessureault, a chartered accountant with the Dessureault, Leblanc, et Lefebvre firm; Paul Lavoie, a consulting economist; Jean Morand, a lawyer with a Master's degree in tax administration, with the Jolicoeur, Lacasse et Simard law firm; Gilles Morin, a chartered accountant; Gabriel Pellerin, a chartered accountant; Luc Therrien, a lawyer with a Master's degree in tax administration with the Baumier & Associes law office, and Laurent Verreault, the Chairman of the Laperriere & Verreault group. Mr. Speaker, there was a meeting of those people in Trois-Rivieres and 1 told them: We are working on a tax reform, and I would like to know what you, as professionals involved daily with such matters, would expect from that reform. And I have just quoted part of their report.

May 28, 1987
Supply
I believe that most Canadians, if presented with those suggestions, would agree with them. Our tax burden is unfairly distributed at the present time, Mr. Speaker. The increase that we have seen in the income tax of ordinary taxpayers is counter-progressive, it acts as a barrier to the economic growth of our regions, our provinces and our country.
If you look at the tax incentive that were granted over the years by the former Government, particularly to businesses, companies, Mr. Speaker, it is amazing to see how a number of those businesses, not many of them, but too many nevertheless, took unfair advantage of tax shelters, those tax shelters which the former Government considered normal, which were provided since 1971, since the last tax reform, over the years, and I remember, Mr. Speaker, seing budgets where we had to deal with heaps of documents, technical papers and so on. With respect to the ordinary taxpayers, the situation was pretty much the same. However, tax shelters were mostly available for high income earners than for Canadians with a lower income. The last point, Mr. Speaker, leaving aside partisan biases, is the federal sales tax-
I remember that in 1978, Mr. Speaker, when I was a student at Sherbrooke University, taking a Master's degree in taxation, our professor used to tell us about the federal sales tax that the Federal Government should change shortly, because it was nonsense. That was in 1978 and the federal sales tax law has not been amended. We are aware of it and we have said it. That tax presently harms our businesses. It kills jobs and that is why this reform is so important. That is why this reform must aim to reduce tax rates of individual taxpayers who have paid too much tax and of corporations which paid their fair share, while increasing the tax rate of corporations which have not paid their share. At the same time, in that comprehensive reform, we should amend the federal sales tax. We have said that we would reduce tax rates and also that we would reduce the number of tax brackets in order to streamline the system. And we said that we would change exemptions which taxpayers enjoy in tax credits.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, a tax credit, whatever its kind and level, is much more profitable than an exemption for a taxpayer. To understand that, you do not have to go to university for it is mathematical. At the same time, it brings about a huge benefit. It makes the tax system more equitable because as you know, Mr. Speaker, if I am entitled to a tax credit of $1,000, somebody whose yearly income is $100,000 will happen to pay more tax than with an exemption for the same amount. As for low income people, of course, they will benefit more from a tax credit than an exemption.
Therefore, all Canadians will eventually pay less tax, thanks to the tax reform. That is the important thing to remember. The White Paper on tax reform will be tabled in that perspective.
Obviously, within that context, high income people who might have avoided to pay their fair share of tax in the past will have to pay more. That is the substance of my basic criteria when I referred to fairness, when I said that all Canadians must pay their fair share of income tax at all levels.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that in terms of tax law, we have innovated in this country with the introduction a federal sales tax credit. It was the first time in this country that a Government, after increasing the rate of the federal sales tax, had the decency to grant a refundable credit to low income people. This is a new kind of law, Mr. Speaker. And I can tell you, having had the opportunity to go to different places in Quebec as well as outside that province, that people are grateful for that. Nobody likes tax increases, but people recognize that, while there has been an increase, this Government has taken steps to help low-income families.

There is nothing to indicate that this new benefit will not resurface in the White Paper.
As far as corporations are concerned, we must put together a package for our corporations which really create jobs in this country, even if the socialist party refuses to believe it. We must see to it that they carry their fair share of the tax burden. We must be careful not to overtax them, however, because they create most jobs in this country, but we must collect the income tax they owe. I suggest that the previous Government's performance in this regard had left a lot to be desired. The White Paper will be there to correct all past mistakes.
As I was saying a while ago, Mr. Speaker, our federal sales tax scheme is much too narrow. As it is currently applied, it favours imported goods at the expense of Canadian goods. This is something which is not right and should be changed, Mr. Speaker.
As a country, Canada needs a federal sales tax scheme with a wider base and reduced rates to be levied more evenly and equitably on a wide variety of goods and services.
There can be different types of federal sales tax. There could be a multi-stage sales tax, with or without invoices, levied only by the federal Government, or a federal provincial sales tax with invoices, but what we should be seeking in a non-partisan way is the common good of Canadians. If the federal government can agree with the 10 provinces, and so far I think that things are going well at this level, to set up a national sales tax scheme, 1 think it would be a great step for Canada, for each and every province and, therefore, for all Canadian taxpayers.
The make-up of the sales tax base will be a key element of our indirect tax system reform and I think that what we should be looking at is the tax reform as a whole. We should take into account personal income taxes, corporate taxes and indirect taxes which is the federal sales tax. I think that if we tried to look at them separately and individually, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre is doing, we would be wrong. This is a major and comprehensive reform. It must not be divided.
May 28, 1987

You are signalling that I am running out of time, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion, I feel that the motion moved today must be defeated and that my friend the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre should wait until we introduce our White Paper on June 18 before making comments which might not reflect reality and, as my other colleague was saying, serve only to frighten Canadians. This is a responsible Government which is seeking a tax reform for the common good of Canadians and, in this context, 1 urge him to wait until June 18.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the question put by my colleague from Montreal-Sainte-Marie, I did not read the above-mentioned report. and given away to Canadian and international corporations already making millions in profits. That seems to me to be much more aberrant.

Finally, he indicates that he is not even willing to attempt to influence his Government to ensure that taxation of food will not be included in the tax reform proposals that the Minister of Finance will submit on June 18.
The Hon. Member is mistaken when he states that the Opposition is against fiscal reform. If he is referring to the New Democratic Party, I submit that our party has been pushing for fiscal reform. I was among the Members of our Party who travelled all across Canada to discuss tax reform with Canadians and to gather information as part of the 1986 Tax Probe project. 1 have recently given speeches on this topic in various communities in Ontario and Quebec. The Hon. Member is therefore mistaken to think that the New Democratic Party is not pushing for tax reform.
But then again, there is such a thing as the wrong kind of fiscal reform. I fear, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Member does not grasp the necessity of voicing a considered opinion on the specific initiative which the Government is proposing, that is to impose a 7 per cent, 8 per cent or 9 per cent tax on all purchases of food and grocery items in Canada.

It should tell us: "Don't ask for our opinions now, wait until we are willing and ready to accept comments." Mr. Speaker, Canadians already know what it means. Member: Is he willing to listen to the people, the poor, those who live below the poverty line, as well as workers who are just beyond the poverty line but do not want, and cannot afford, a tax on the necessities of life like bread and milk?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I refuse to get involved in the Hon. Member's little games. Considering the kind of speech he made, no wonder he is ashamed and wants to make a quick exit.
Mr. Speaker, I fully realize the disastrous situation facing the Conservatives today, and I realize why the Hon. Member would prefer to disappear without a trace, because that is exactly what is going to happen to him in the next election. I understand that, and I support the motion and what was said in the debate today by the New Democratic Party.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians, including the senior citizens, mothers and workers who are watching us today, remember clearly the solemn commitment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), with one hand on his heart and the other on the Bible, when he promised full indexation of Old Age Security pensions. People remember the so-called consultation. It is true that this Government consults, but then it turns around and does the exact opposite. It misleads people. I have here the January 1985 Consultation Paper signed by the Minister of National Health and "Social Injustice" in Canada, who told senior citizens: Nothing will be changed. Don't worry. Remember the Mulroney Budget! What happened? Old Age Security pensions were de-indexed. He told families: Don't worry, the changes that are going to be made in support programs for families with children, including family allowance, the child tax credit and the child tax exemption, will not
Supply
be used to reduce the deficit but to help people in need. Again, Canadians and this House were deceived by the Government. Six months later, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was forced to admit that he had cut, in fact had stolen money from Canadian families to reduce his deficit and at the same time, given the rich a capital gains tax exemption of $500,000. What Alain Dubuc, in yesterday's La Presse, referred to as "Capital gains: an obscene giveaway", is indeed an obscene giveaway, useless except for making the rich richer. It does not create a single job for anyone, and today, the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres and his fellow Members of the Conservative Party are saying: How come, you are making people scared? But the Conservative Members misled Canadians. You misled them on four occasions, yet now you expect them to believe you. They will never believe you from now on. When it comes to the tax reform Canadians insist that Conservative Members who have enough courage and this Prime Minister who misled them four times tell them that food, which is essential to survive, will not be taxed.
Still the Conservative Members are asking themselves: How come people have lost faith in us? How come people do not listen to us? Why is it that people no longer trust us? Simple: This same Government came out with a Budget to remove indexation on Old Age Security pensions and family allowances, and then decided to slap a 10 per cent tax on prescription drugs, taxing the health of people yet. Mr. Speaker, 1 too wish to enter into debate on the motion presented by my Party. The motion calls upon the Government not to impose a federal tax on food. This motion is presented at a time when we are about ready to enter into a regime of tax reform. Certainly, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has given every indication that there will be some form of federal sales tax, whether it will be called a business-transfer tax or a value-added tax, the type of tax which most European countries now have, or whether it will be a federal sales tax, and that is a tax in conjunction with the provinces. Regardless of the form this sales tax will take, there is very good reason to believe that food will be taxed by the federal Government.
My colleagues and I in the New Democratic Party basically oppose this measure. Let me say that there is no doubt that we need reform of our tax system. We also need reform of our federal sales and excise tax system. The system as it exists today is in many ways confusing and arbitrary. While the Government has set rates, we also know that the Department of Revenue enters into numerous contracts with various firms and establishes other rates. I think it is just a question of time before some of those agreements are taken to court because some industries have these agreements and other industries have other agreements. Certainly some people claim that these agreements are arbitrary.
I have received correspondence from business people who feel the federal sales tax which was imposed on their product was unfair. In fact, I am dealing with a particular case right now where federal sales tax was imposed and then two or three years later the Government admitted it had made a mistake and refunded all the money which had been collected by this particular manufacturer. It did not do the manufacturer much good because over a period of years he had to charge the sales tax and he succeeded in pricing his goods out of the market because his competitors did not have to pay that sales tax. This individual lost a fair amount of business. In fact, the particular business he was involved in has since gone bankrupt.
I do not have to be convinced that the sales tax regime which now exists is in need of reform. It is, as I mentioned, very arbitrary and confusing. I remember meeting a while ago

May 28, 1987
Supply
with manufacturers of sailboats in Victoria. They told me that various items on their boats were taxed at different levels and different rates. It was very confusing for them. Certainly, our present sales tax regime imposes taxes on our exporters and gives some benefit to importers. Canada is one of the few countries in the world that actually gives benefit to those who import. We tax those who export. This is because of our particular system, which just does not make sense.
It has been known for quite some time that our sales tax system is a total mess. In the many years that the Liberals were in power they really did not do very much to clean it up. In fact, if anything, they added to it.
I understand that if we are to have a sales tax of some sort, it is desirable that it be as simple as possible. Some European countries have value-added taxes that really impose a high level of bureaucracy upon the businesses that have to collect it.
I think it is in the interests of everyone that if we must have a sales tax in Canada, it be as simple as possible.
I certainly do not disagree with the attempt of the Government to reform our tax system, in particular the sales tax system, to end up with a simple system, one that is easy to administer and understand. There is no doubt that if we are to have a simple system then tax must be placed on everything. The moment one starts to introduce exemptions then one starts to create more paperwork. I understand that.
I understand the notion that if one is to have simplicity, then quite often it has to be at the expense of equity. If one is to have equity then one has to introduce some form of complexity into the tax system. This is true whether we are talking about sales tax or income tax. There is a trade-off that Governments have to make between simplicity and fairness. Of course, a wise government attempts to have as simple a system as possible while having a primarily fair system.
Thus I come to the following point. I have admitted that we need reform of our tax system, in particular the sales tax system. I have admitted that the more exemptions one introduces into a federal sales tax system the more complexity there is created. However, I have to rise here in my place today to oppose the imposition of a federal sales tax on food. I rise today to denounce any attempt to tax food. I do this for the following reasons.
All those who advocate a federal sales tax recognize that it is regressive. The Minister of Finance has stated both in the House and in committee, as well as in other public fora, that, yes, a sales tax is a regressive measure. It is regressive because everyone pays the same per centage of tax on an item regardless of one's ability to pay. Thus a person who buys a steak, a pound of hamburger, or a can of sardines pays the same tax, whatever the rate might be. Of course, a poor person who has to dispose of most of his income on the basic necessities of life, that is, food, shelter and clothing, ends up paying a proportionately higher per centage of his income as a tax than a person
with more income. Therefore it is regressive. I think that with this basic principle there is surely no disagreement.
Everyone will recognize that a federal sales tax, or a provincial sales tax, is a regressive form of taxation. It is not tied to one's ability to pay. However, the Minister of Finance stated that he would correct this. He said, "We are going to introduce a federal sales tax credit". He pointed to the fact that the 1985 Budget created a federal sales tax credit so that those people who are at the low end of the income scale will receive a credit back. In other words, the money they have spent on the essentials for goods and services which they need and upon which they have paid federal sales tax will be partially reimbursed through this sales tax credit.
The credit amounts to some $50 for a person and then $25 for every dependant under the age of 18. The maximum income that a family of four could earn in order to qualify is around $15,000 per year. As soon as that family earns more than $15,000 per year then the tax credit will be reduced accordingly. If the family earns up to $18,000 per year then they will not get anything back. They will not get any credit at all.
It has to be recognized that the sales tax credit the Minister of Finance and the Government have given does not compensate what a family of four at the low end of the income scale would be paying the Government in federal sales tax and excise tax. First, the $50 does not cover it. Okay, I will accept the fact that that is sort of a first step. I would have greater difficulty rising in my place today to oppose a sales tax on food had the Minister of Finance in his Budget of February of this year indicated that the Government would maintain the sales tax credit at some equal level. I would have more difficulty if he had said that as the amount individuals pay and as the sales tax goes up he would increase the credit for poorer families. He failed to do that. He failed to index the level at which people would become eligible for the sales tax credit; and he did not index the sales tax credit itself. In fact, he increased the sales tax in his Budget. He increased the amount that he was taking in from Canadian consumers. He increased the tax on gasoline. He added more items to the list of those which will be taxed by the federal sales tax. Therefore, he is taking more money out of the pockets of Canadian consumers. However, he did not compensate or increase the compensation to the poor by increasing the sales tax credit.
In my books the Minister committed three sins. First, he did not index the level at which people would become eligible for the sales tax credit. Second, he did not index the sales tax credit. Third, he did not increase the sales tax credit when he increased the sales tax.
If the Government is to introduce a wide sales tax on all goods and services, and if it wants to convince the Canadian public that the very poor will be compensated for this increase in taxation, then the Minister should have sent out a signal to the people that whatever benefits they will get back will not be eroded. He did not do that. The whole matter comes down to a
May 28, 1987

question of trust. I for one do not have trust in the Government, nor does the Canadian public, particularly the poor, have any trust or confidence in it. We are concerned that the Minister of Finance will impose a sales tax, especially on the basic needs; food, clothing and shelter. Will he at the same time redress the imbalance, the unfairness and the inequity of the federal sales tax by giving a tax credit to the poor? We cannot believe that a tax credit would be fully indexed, so it would in time just erode, erode and erode. Certainly the Minister of Finance can introduce a Budget, impose a federal sales tax and then compensate the very poor with a tax credit. But then a year later with inflation and an increase in the federal sales tax, what will happen? The people who would be eligible to receive the sales tax credit would become fewer in number. In a few years time the benefit would hardly be meaningful.
If Canadians are to accept that the inequity of a federal sales tax will be redressed by a federal tax credit, then Canadians will have to be able to trust the Government that the tax credit will remain constant with the cost of living. Canadians will have to trust the Government that there will be full indexing. We do not have the confidence in this Government to do that.
We have seen this Government more often than not break its sacred trust. We saw that with the attempt to deindex the benefits to pensioners. Were it not for the opposition of senior citizens across the country and the Opposition in this House, the Government would have succeeded in deindexing benefits to our old people. The Government succeeded in deindexing the family allowance and the family child tax credit so that fewer and fewer people are now qualified to receive those benefits. It is an eroding base.
I hear an Hon. Member say, "We will give it all away". Member says, "We will give it all away", that has been happening both under Liberal and Tory Governments. We have been giving it away, but we have not been giving it to the poor. be made without producing one cent of tax. Isn't that shameful, Mr. Speaker? Is that fair? Is that equal? We say no. Let me give you an idea of what the Manitoba New Democratic Government did and how much the people of Manitoba trust that Government.
Concerning the taxing of food, a question which the Hon. Member raised, the Manitoba NDP Government's Budget this year raised taxes through provincial sales tax on take-out orders. The Manitoba New Democratic Government has taxed food. The NDP Government in Manitoba has gone further. It now taxes water. The headlines in the paper read, "What next? A tax on the air that we breath?" Now in Manitoba the provincial NDP Government taxes municipalities for the use of water from the rivers, the rivers that were formed from rain that drains off the land which the people own. This is what we can expect from an NDP Government.
The Hon. Member talks about the fairness of sales tax. In Manitoba, the New Democratic Party Government raised the sales tax by 1 per cent and took away the sales tax credit that the federal Government gave the seniors through the federal sales tax exemption credit. The Manitoba NDP Government took that away.
Who do we trust, Mr. Speaker? Do we trust the Hon. Member for Regina East? The Member talks about not indexing certain things. In Manitoba you pay 2 per cent tax on your net income. Do you know what that means, Mr. Speaker? Does the Hon. Member from Regina East know what that means to senior citizens and to families? When you tax net income, you do not take into account basic personal deductions, family size, age or charitable donations. But that NDP Government does not even take into account the disability or the pension deduction. This is what the NDP Manitoba Government did. Who can we trust when you get something like that happening?
Can we trust the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre when he said, "Don't cut spending, tax higher". That is exactly what the NDP Government did in Manitoba. Mr. Speaker, we have a unique tax in Manitoba called the payroll tax. It was increased by 50 per cent, from 1.5 per cent to 2.25 per cent. If one decides to open a business and create 30 jobs in Manitoba, one must pay 2.25 per cent of employees' salaries in taxes to the provincial Government. Does the Hon. Member for Regina East support that principle?
We want to broaden the base in our tax reform so that lower individual income taxes will be paid by both persons and corporations. We are hoping for and encouraging investment
in our country to create jobs, which is the reverse effect of the direction taken by the Manitoba Government that has increased by 50 per cent the amount of tax people who are opening businesses will have to pay from their employees' incomes.
Does the Hon. Member support that type of taxation? Would he institute it if his Party were the Government of Canada?

subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in some ways we already have an employment tax. Certainly CPP and UI contributions are in one form or another a payroll tax per se. Governments must raise revenues. It does not matter what Party forms the Government, whether it be NDP, Conservative, or Liberal. The question is one of fairness-what is fair and what produces the best economic results. Certainly we could say that a certain measure is an undesirable tax and that it would be better if we did not have it. Certainly the cost of doing business in Canada would be much less if there was no necessity for CPP and unemployment insurance contributions.
If Manitoba did not have its payroll tax, the money would have to be raised from other sources of revenue. However, it is within the ability of the federal Government to set up a tax regime. Surely that is where the action must lie. If the federal Government shows leadership in introducing a fair tax regime, many provinces would also see their tax revenues increase.
I should like to pose a question to the Hon. Member. Does he think it is fair that, for example, in 1983 the Royal Bank of Canada, with over $360 million in profits, did not pay one cent of tax? In fact, the Royal Bank of Canada received a tax credit of some $25 million. Is that fair? No, it is not. No wonder we are running into deficits. No wonder there is a squeeze on many provincial Governments to make up the difference through regressive tax measures.
If the taxation system in the country were fair, provincial revenues would likely increase as well and the need for regressive taxes would become less. Had we had a fair tax regime in the country, there would not have been the need for the Government to increase sales taxes, as it has in the last number of years. We would have come close to balanced budgets, had those with the ability to pay actually been paying their fair share of tax. When the largest corporations in Canada can make over $13 billion in profits in one year and not pay one cent of tax, something is very wrong, very sick, very unfair.
We will support the Government in its attempt to correct that measure, but adding a tax on food will not do it. It is not the type of tax reform we will support. In the area of genuine tax reform, by golly, we are right behind the Government and applaud it, but we cannot support regressive tax reform.
May 28, 1987

My wife will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I even have trouble balancing our own family cheque-book. However, I am an individual who has been paying income tax in Canada for a couple of decades at least, and it is to my fellow taxpayers that I wish to direct my remarks this afternoon.

I hate to disagree with one of my own colleagues, but the Deputy Government House Leader this morning said when the motion was brought forward that it was "an appropriate motion for debate". I do not think it is. It is an interesting

The NDP and the Liberals set up these strawmen and then knock them down. They spent a whole day of House time knocking down strawmen, and I think it is an absolute waste of time. speechtext:
I should like to thank my colleagues for their comments, but I will resume debate.
Following June 18 when the White Paper is presented, we will have more meat to chew on, so to speak, and we should be able to have ample opportunity to debate the question. However, a White Paper is just that; it is a discussion paper, an opportunity for the Government to put forward its ideas. At that time we can certainly deal with the question of taxes on whatever items.
As I rose to join in the debate today, my eye caught the sculpture on the west wall of the House of Commons which reads: "Impot-Tax", and below it is depicted a Canadian family. There is a father, a mother, and a child on the lap. I am sure that when this Chamber was built, that was put there for good reason. Those are the commoners of Canada, the people who make what we do possible through their taxation dollars. Indeed, the figure appears on one of the major arches of the House of Commons, quite appropriately. If it was not there, the ceiling would fall down. Those people are important to Canada. They are the ones who make what we do possible and it is to them that I wish to address my remarks today.
Let me begin by making an obvious but important assumption. Where the tax system is concerned, fairness is uppermost in the minds of most Canadians. Fairness is the basic standard by which Canadians assess the tax system and how it affects them and others around them.
Over the past decade, the perception has grown that the tax system falls short of the level of fairness Canadians have a right to expect. This growing perception is expressed in questions any Canadian might ask: why is the tax burden so high, why do some people in the same circumstances pay less

May 28, 1987
Supply
tax, how is it that some profitable corporations pay little or no tax?
The latter question was raised in debate by my hon. colleague from Regina East. He asked if it was right that the Royal Bank of Canada with all its profits pay no tax. It is not right and that is the purpose of tax reform. Tax reform will ensure that corporations like that pay their fair share. I cannot understand why members of the NDP and the Liberal Party would oppose tax reform.
The Government shares the concerns of most Canadians about the tax system. We intend, in the weeks and months to come, to make the Canadian taxation system fairer. We believe that the tax system should not only be fair but that it should generally be perceived to be fair. We believe it is a primary responsibility to ensure that the elderly and those in greatest need receive fair treatment. We believe that high-income earners and profitable corporations should pay their fair share of tax. We believe that individuals with similar abilities to pay taxes should pay similar amounts of tax. Finally, we believe that fair sharing of the tax burden should apply broadly across sectors of the economy and across goods and services.
Ironically, one of my constituents came up with what he thought was the perfect solution to all of our tax dilemmas. He suggested, in all due respect, that we should consider taxing sex. He said that indeed, if a tax was paid whenever the act was performed, eventually Canadians would brag about how much they were paying in taxes and indeed we would solve all of our deficit problems. It would be a little hard to administer, but like most of my constituents' suggestions, one worth considering.
For the third time in 20 years Canadians will soon attempt a major overhaul of the tax system. It is generally agreed that the first two attempts by other Governments ended in failure. In each case, the blueprint for tax reform designed by economists and tax specialists was shredded by the arguments and opposition of special-interest groups who sought to maintain the tax preferences that benefited them most.
The greatest challenge facing proponents of comprehensive tax reform today, proponents like members of the Government, is the same as it was in the past. It is to reform the tax system to make it internationally competitive, fair and efficient in a way that avoids the swamp of special-interest pleading. Avoiding the swamp will require not only a sound blueprint for reform, which we will soon release, but also a Government that is prepared to consult on ways to improve that reform and will provide the leadership necessary to see that the national interest is put ahead of special interests. The Government we have in Canada today is that kind of Government.
Last summer, the U.S. Congress made history when it passed its comprehensive tax reform Bill. So many things in Canada are dependent upon what happens south of the 49th. That is the world in which we live. By eliminating hundreds of deductions and incentives, the Americans were able to
substantially reduce personal and corporate income tax rates for the first time in decades. The Canadian Government has now served notice that it too is planning an overhaul of its entire tax system.
We in Canada have lived with taxation for over 300 years. The first recorded tax in Canada was levied in 1650. It was an export tax on beaver and moose pelts. The annual revenue yield is estimated to have been no more than $200. If the Liberals had been in power then, they might have received $200 and spent $300, but that is another matter.
In 1867, the British North America Act institutionalized taxation by granting the federal Government wide powers to raise revenues while restricting the provinces to direct taxation within their own jurisdictional boundaries. Direct taxation includes such taxes as personal and corporate income tax, property tax, sales tax, succession duties, et cetera. Customs and excise taxes are the best examples of indirect taxation.
In 1916, the business profits war tax Act was passed to help finance the Canadian war effort followed by the income war tax Act in 1917. That was, of course, the first national personal income tax and it was, we were told then, a temporary measure. For the next 20 years, the bulk of government revenues continued to be derived from customs and excise taxes on products such as tobacco and alcohol. By the time World War II started, however, the burden of taxation had shifted to personal and corporate income taxes.
Governments have continually tinkered with the Income Tax Act for the past 40 years. Changes have been made under the guise of stimulating economic growth, creating employment and increasing international competitiveness as well as more equitably redistributing income. Forty years of changes during which the Conservatives have only been in power for five or six years means that the Liberals must take credit for 35 of those 40 years. Those changes have made the Act one of the most unwieldy, complex pieces of legislation today.
The Canadian Income Tax Act is about as thick as three volumes of Hansard and some say it makes just about as much sense. There is also a generally accepted feeling that the current system no longer meets the stated objectives. The question of fairness figures prominently in people's perception of our current tax system. Public opinion indicates that there is a growing attitudinal gap between those in the upper and lower ends of the socio-economic scale. Those on the lower end have the sense that while the economy may be steadily improving, they are not benefiting from it. Much of that feeling can be traced back to concerns about the tax system and the belief that corporations are not paying their fair share due to the numerous deductions and exemptions available.
These exemptions and deductions for corporations, of course, do serve a valuable purpose. Corporations do hire people. William Watson of McGill University, in the March 26 edition of the Financial Post, said:
The corporation is nothing more than a convenient legal fiction. Corporations
don't pay taxes. People pay corporate taxes. The taxes are paid either by the
corporation's customers (in higher prices), by its workers (in lower wages), by
May 28, 1987

its suppliers (in lower materials prices), or by its shareholders (in reduced earnings).
Unfortunately, 50 years of economic analysis hasn't made clear in just what proportion these four groups pay ... more and more corporations are now owned by pension plans, so that, increasingly, even when "capital" pays, labor pays. If the NDP wants to raise a tax that may well be paid in large part by the "working class," that's fine by me, though someone should tell the working class what its friends are up to.
Indeed, when we talk about the value of corporations and small business to the Canadian economy, we should remember where our recent economic growth has come from. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business points out the following:
Solid growth has been achieved with an 11 per cent increase in business formations over 1984, a net gain of 65,000 new businesses. The marked improvement in national job generation has resulted in a significant lowering of unemployment.
That is something for which my colleagues and I will take some credit. The federation continues:
Over 70 per cent of the jobs created during this Government's mandate, in excess of 394,000, are the result of small business entrepreneurial activity.
Of course, that is also the result of good Government. The federation goes on to say:
Canadians in all regions are benefiting from the hard work of the nation's risk takers who have been encouraged by measures in the last two budgets.
Those measures will be improved by the measures contained in the White Paper on tax reform which is to be released on June 18.
With all that in mind, we cannot deny that by treating different sources of investment and savings in different ways, financial decisions by corporations and individuals are often made purely on the basis of tax treatment.
A good example of tax abuse, as we have heard several times in the Chamber today, is the scientific research tax credit introduced in 1983 to encourage research. It ended up costing the federal Treasury $3 billion or $4 billion without a proportionate amount of scientific research being done. The result is that the Government and taxpayers have been subsidizing companies without enjoying the full benefits of job creation, regional development or indeed scientific breakthroughs.
The Minister of Finance first addressed the issue of tax reform in his economic statement of 1984. This is culminating in the White Paper of June 18. Indeed, a background paper prepared for the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs by the C. D. Howe Institute issued a warning to which my opposition colleagues should pay heed. The institute said:
Much of the debate undoubtedly will be couched in terms of the reform's fairness. In this regard, we believe that it is essential to focus on the impact of the over-all package rather than on individual elements. Failure to judge the reform in this way may mean that special interests will dominate, to the detriment of the national interest.
Supply
We must have a release of that White Paper, and deal with the measures it contains then, not 20 days in advance, as we are doing today.
How will our Government make Canada's taxation system fair? Let us look first at lower rates. Lower marginal rates coupled with the elimination of preferences, and strengthened provisions to counter tax avoidance, would reverse our growing dependence on personal income taxes. Canadians would get to keep more of each additional dollar they earn to spend, save or invest as they choose. They would also be assured that others are bearing their fair share of the burden. I repeat, fair taxation will make tax reform work.
What has our Government done so far to improve our taxation system? As has been mentioned several times today, we put an end to the SRTC which was considerably abused. We restricted tax losses and credits for investors and limited partnerships. We put a stop to the so-called carve-out transactions in the oil and gas sector. We introduced rules to prevent trading in tax losses and credits among corporations. We also brought in the minimum income tax, the sales tax credit, and increases in the child tax credit.
A major part of our continuing tax reform will be to build in several specific measures to ensure that low-income Canadians, including pensioners, are treated equitably. I trust the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) is listening because many pensioners will go off the tax rolls because of the tax reform we are bringing in.
As part of our tax reform we are going to convert personal exemptions and some deductions to tax credits. Exemptions favour those in higher income brackets. Indeed, the identical exemption confers considerably more benefit on the high-income earner as it is now, than on the lower income earner. On the other hand, a tax credit provides the same dollar benefit to taxpayers regardless of their income level. With a system of tax credits, lower income taxpayers will receive greater benefit than they do now, while those at the higher income levels would receive less.
A system of tax credits would make the system more progressive. In other words, for every $1,000 of tax exemption the individual at the 34 per cent rate is allowed a $340 tax exemption. The lower income earner at the bottom of the scale, 6 per cent, only makes $60 on that exemption. That is what we are changing through the tax credit system. With the change from exemptions to credits, many low-income people, including pensioners, will be dropped from the rolls. These people will no longer be required to pay income tax.
Let there be no doubt at all about the Government's revenue intentions for tax reform. We have said all along that in pursuing a fairer balance our intention is to ensure a sounder, more predictable revenue base, not greater total revenue. Tax reform will not be a tax grab. That is worth repeating. Tax reform under a Progressive Conservative Government will not be a tax grab.

May 28, 1987
Supply
To sum up, the Government's plan for comprehensive tax reform is to bring greater equity to the federal taxation system. We want Canadians to feel that their tax system treats ail members of the Canadian community fairly. When you analyse all the features of the tax reform, all the improvements we want to make are designed to ultimately improve the fairness of the system. We realize that a fair tax system, fair in the fullest sense of the word, is one that helps the economy to operate to its full potential at maximum efficiency, so that it generates the growth and produces the jobs which will benefit all Canadians. A tax system that does that is a system of which all Canadians can be proud. This is our goal in tax reform and we intend to accomplish it.
The public debate on tax reform is just beginning to build momentum. The search for an equitable tax system acceptable to all Canadians, including the provinces, the business community and social groups, will be one of the most difficult tasks this Government will face. However, failure to do so will only perpetuate a problem which has simply become too expensive to ignore. We will act. We will reform the tax system. Canadian taxpayers expect it, want it, and they are going to get tax reform under a Progressive Conservative Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been an interesting and perhaps a bit disturbing kind of debate, given the submissions made by government Members. 1 say disturbing because through the entire day those Members talked about tax reform in general terms. They suggested we should have a debate on tax reform in general. They have avoided the specific question put before the House, which is that the House declare itself in opposition to the imposition of a federal tax on food and urges the Government to reject such a tax as part of its tax reform package.
The Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schelien-berg) has joined the chorus of those who say how wonderful tax reform is while avoiding the question of whether or not it is appropriate to levy a tax on people's grocery bills. This is particularly important to those working Canadians who are somewhere not too far above what we see now as the poverty line in major cities and are still struggling to make end's meet. They may occasionally take their kids to McDonald's or do something special for them rather than just grimly hanging on. They will be really hit by a $400 or $500 a year tax on their grocery bill. That is what the business-transfer tax proposal would amount to. If the precedent established with respect to the sales tax were followed they would get no remission of that tax at all.
Perhaps I can ask the Hon. Member to answer the question directly. Does he favour a tax on food or is he prepared to join with us and express his reservations over imposing a tax on the most basic essential of life.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presume the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre enjoys dealing with hypothetical situations. I do not. He was not here at the beginning of my speech when I said I have yet to see-
