speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that sums up the problem. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and others have on many occasions averred to a major new tax area which I believe most Canadians would find objectionable. It is clear that such a tax would be extremely regressive even if a modest amount of tax credit were given to low-income Canadians.
A month ago I was briefed by the Department of Finance at length on the business-transfer tax which, as I understand it, is still the most likely option to be implemented. It was referred to by the Minister of Finance in his statement in this House on May 6. I will just refer to a departmental analysis in order to inform the Hon. Member and explain why I am expressing my Party's concerns now rather than waiting tamely and passively until the afternoon of June 18. Even then we will still be in the dark because the proposals are being put forward at eight p.m. in the evening.
This is from an analysis the Department of Finance made just a month ago. They said ad hoc changes would be complex and limited in scope. A shift to the wholesale level would be rejected by business. A shift to the retail level is not feasible in the presence of provincial retail sales taxes. The business-transfer tax is feasible "only if applied at a single rate and on all goods and services". That is what the Government is considering. The BTT is a comprehensive tax with few exemptions. It is not viable with exemptions at multiple rates. Exemptions lead to double taxation and complicate compliance and administration, and the impact on lower income families is best redressed through a tax credit.
We have a proposal for a tax on food with no exemption and a credit for low-income families. The Government has defined low-income families as those earning less than $15,000 a year. There is a gap of about $5,000 a year below the urban poverty line for a family of four in which people would be paying the tax on food. This is not hypothetical. This is a very real proposal which is currently being considered by the Ministry
May 28, 1987

and is being actively lobbied for by the tax experts and officials in the Department of Finance.
Is the Member prepared to stand with me and other Members of Parliament in telling the Government that that is not an acceptable form of tax and that it should rule that out and look for other options for reform of the sales tax? Is the Hon. Member prepared to say that or not?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82  TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext: Here we go again, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Centre has gone to a briefing where items were thrown out which may or may not be acted upon. He is taking up a day's time on a situation which I continue to call a strawman, a hypothetical windmill at which he wants to tilt. 1 have discussed a number of the measures which may or may not come forward in tax reform. Knowing the Minister of Finance as I do, I am sure he will take the wisdom and the excellent advice of the Member for Nanaimo-Alberni to heart and we will all see that on June 18.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82  TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has quite rightly been trying to enlighten the House, notwithstanding the fact that many Members of the House have indicated that they will probably still be in the dark after the White Paper has been issued. I know the Hon. Member is concerned about the complexity and the arbitrary nature of the current federal sales tax provisions. I know that he is as concerned as I am about the fact, for example, that fluoridated toothpaste may qualify as a tax-exempt health product because it claims to be fighting cavities, or it may be taxable as a cosmetic. That is an example of the problems which the current federal sales tax imposes on our system.
In his statement the Minister of Finance indicated that there are a number of options for dealing with this particular issue. He indicated that one of the options which would be put forward is a business transfer tax. He also indicated that we could still have a federal sales tax. In addition, he talked about the possibility of a combined federal and provincial sales tax which appears to be a good option.
Would the Hon. Member comment on the three options, and particularly on what the chances are that we may have a combined provincial and federal sales tax, bearing in mind that the Province of Alberta currently has no provincial sales tax? I have been told by some people in the eastern part of British Columbia, the Hon. Member's home province, that at one time there was a movement afoot to secede to Alberta because there is no sales tax paid there while there is in the Hon. Member's province.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82  TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext:
I would like to thank my hon. colleague for his question. It seems that very often westerners are talking about seceding from one body or another. That often happens when they get disgruntled. That is the way we are.
The Hon. Member is correct when he talks about how the federal sales tax kills jobs. We are told that Canada's federal sales tax is the only commodity tax in the world which favours imports over domestic goods. I understand that on average
Royal Assent
Canadian manufacturers pay one-third more tax than competing importers. In fact, some pay as much as 60 or 70 per cent more under the federal sales tax system which now exists than do their important competitors. This happens because the tax is levied on a domestic manufacturers' final price which usually includes expenses for advertising, warehousing, warranty programs and other marketing operations.
My colleague spoke about the different options being considered, such as the business-transfer tax, the federal sales tax, and perhaps a joint federal-provincial sales tax. That shows the kind of consultation which has taken place and the work the Finance Minister, his Department, and my colleagues have done to study all the avenues open. They have consulted and received as much input as possible to ensure that when the announcement is made on June 18 at eight o'clock Ottawa time, 5 p.m. in B.C., it will be the best possible document that we can provide.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82  TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the statement of the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) regarding the tax reform package, he indicated that it was very likely that there would be much more reliance on tax credits than there has been in the past. He indicated as well that the tax credit was a fairer process than deductions, that deductions might very well save high-income persons more taxes than the same deductions would save a low-income person. He indicated that the tax credit system would be more beneficial. Perhaps the Hon. Member can tell us whether he favours a system with tax credits as opposed to deductions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82  TAX REFORM-OPPOSITION TO FOOD TAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. The Hon. Member is correct when he talks about the unfairness of the exemption versus tax credit system. In reality the present tax exemption system is Robin Hood in reverse, it is taxing the poor and giving to the rich. An individual in the 34 per cent bracket who is claiming a tax deduction of $1,000 is getting $340. The individual in the 6 per cent bracket is only getting $60. The Government proposes to remove the tax exemptions and replace them with tax credits in many areas. I think that is a worthy goal.
